category: Topic, reference, respect, role, and capacity

entries.meaning: The preposition of staying current. Its object is not the subject of a statement but the subject somebody is trying to keep up with, which is why it lives among verbs of maintenance and almost never stands alone.
examples: Part of the job is keeping abreast of changes in the tax code.
She reads two trade journals to stay abreast of the industry.
The Friday memo exists to keep the board abreast of the negotiations.
He has never been abreast of what his own department is doing.
Regulators struggled to remain abreast of the new products.
Nobody in the room was abreast of the overnight filings.
entries.pronunciation note: uh-BREST-uv · the stress sits on -breast and never moves; the a- reduces to /ə/ in every register, and final of goes /əv/ → /ə/ before a consonant
entries.русский: в курсе (чего-л.) — только с keep/stay: следить за тем, что меняется
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (abreast of filing on time — grammatical but stiff), or a fused wh-nominal (abreast of what the competition is charging); never a finite that-clause (✗ abreast of that the rules changed → abreast of the change in the rules). The phrase is an adjectival complement rather than a free adverbial, so a verb of maintaining almost always stands in front of it — keep, stay, remain, get, or bring someone — and ✗ I abreast of the news is not a sentence.
entries.pattern: [keep / stay / remain / get] abreast of [noun phrase] · [keep / bring] [object] abreast of [noun phrase] · [noun] abreast of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Against about and on, which merely name a subject, abreast of names a subject somebody is staying current on. It entails a moving target and a continuing effort, which is why keep abreast of the litigation works and ✗ keep abreast of the Battle of Hastings does not — the battle has stopped changing. The informal American equivalent is up on (up on the news); the formal one is current with. Cross-class test — the object: with an object it is this preposition; with nothing after it, abreast is a bare adverb of position (they rode two abreast) and governs nothing at all.
entries.senses treated elsewhere: this entry covers only the "informed about" sense. The spatial one — a moving thing drawing level with a fixed one, as in the tug came abreast of the pier — belongs with the prepositions of place and position.
entries.see also: about, on, on the subject of, in connection with, aware of, familiar with

entries.meaning: The most useful preposition in this file and the default for every job the others do. It is also one of the most polysemous words in English, and only the first three senses below are topic senses.
examples: It's a documentary about two brothers who rebuilt a lighthouse.
She wouldn't tell me anything about the interview.
He's still upset about the parking ticket.
I'm excited about starting the new job.
This isn't about the money — it's about being taken seriously.
Good teaching is about knowing when to stay quiet.
Go about your business and don't stare.
While you're about it, could you refill the ice tray?
There were toys lying about the living room.
He spent the morning wandering about the museum.
There were about forty people in the room.
We got there about nine.
The trip takes about an hour and a half.
There was nobody about when we pulled in.
Nobody knows how the change came about.
She was about to leave when the phone rang.

senses.head: Subject matter
body: What a book, conversation, film, or complaint is on.
examples: It's a documentary about two brothers who rebuilt a lighthouse.
She wouldn't tell me anything about the interview.

senses.head: The target of a feeling or attitude
body: What the emotion is pointed at.
examples: He's still upset about the parking ticket.
I'm excited about starting the new job.

senses.head: The essential point or nature of something
body: Usually in a corrective sentence.
examples: This isn't about the money — it's about being taken seriously.
Good teaching is about knowing when to stay quiet.

senses.head: Occupied with, engaged in
body: A limited, slightly old-fashioned use.
examples: Go about your business and don't stare.
While you're about it, could you refill the ice tray?

senses.head: Here and there within an area
body: Chiefly British; American English uses around, and British round is not an American option at all.
examples: There were toys lying about the living room.
He spent the morning wandering about the museum.

senses.head: Not a preposition — the degree modifier "approximately."
body: It has no object; it just sits in front of a number or a measurement.
examples: There were about forty people in the room.
We got there about nine.
The trip takes about an hour and a half.

senses.head: Not a preposition — the adverb and the verb particle
body: Nothing follows for it to govern, and in be about to it is frozen into an idiom of imminence.
examples: There was nobody about when we pulled in.
Nobody knows how the change came about.
She was about to leave when the phone rang.

entries.pronunciation note: uh-BOWT · the stressed second syllable never reduces; only the unstressed first one drops
entries.русский: о, об — тема книги, разговора, жалобы; перед числом — «около, примерно»
entries.type: simple (historically a fusion of Old English on + būtan "outside") — also an adverb (there was nobody about), a degree modifier (about forty), and a verb particle (bring it about, come about)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, gerund (about starting the job), or a wh-clause (about what happened, about whether to go, about how it works) — never a bare that-clause (✗ I told her about that the meeting moved). To carry a that-clause you must insert a noun: about the fact that she left. As an adverb or particle it takes no object at all.
entries.pattern: [verb] about [noun phrase] · [noun] about [noun phrase] · [adjective] about [noun phrase] · stranded: the thing I told you about · fronted and formal: the matter about which we spoke
entries.contrast: Against on, about is the general, conversational topic word and on is the scholarly one: a book about bees is for anyone, a book on bees is a treatise. On also implies sustained, organized treatment, which is why you can give a lecture on Keats but only a quick word about your weekend. Against over, about is neutral where over implies a fight. The "scattered here and there" sense (papers lying about the room) is British; American English says around, and British round is not an American option. Cross-class test — the object: we talked about the merger is the preposition (object the merger); there was nobody about and about forty people are adverbs with nothing after them to govern; bring it about is a particle, where the object it belongs to bring; and be about to is a fixed idiom in which about governs nothing and cannot be moved or stranded.
entries.see also: on, over, regarding, concerning, on the subject of, of

entries.meaning: Introduces the matter an official communication is about. Unlike the participial prepositions of cause (considering, given), it has lost every trace of its verb: no subject is implied and nothing is doing any concerning.
examples: I'm writing concerning the invoice dated March 4.
The committee received two complaints concerning the same instructor.
Concerning your request for an extension, the deadline is fixed by statute.
The statute is silent concerning leases signed before 1998.
There is no documentation concerning who authorized the transfer.
She refused to answer questions concerning her time at the agency.
The trend in the third quarter is concerning.
Two of the lab values came back concerning enough to repeat.

senses.head: The subject of an inquiry, complaint, or official communication
body: The core sense, and the reason the word survives in correspondence at all.
examples: I'm writing concerning the invoice dated March 4.
The committee received two complaints concerning the same instructor.
Concerning your request for an extension, the deadline is fixed by statute.

senses.head: The matter a document, rule, or statute covers — or conspicuously fails to cover
body: Very common after silent, vague, no documentation, no provision.
examples: The statute is silent concerning leases signed before 1998.
There is no documentation concerning who authorized the transfer.
She refused to answer questions concerning her time at the agency.

senses.head: Not a preposition — the modern adjective meaning "worrying."
body: It governs nothing, follows a linking verb freely, and takes degree modifiers the preposition cannot.
examples: The trend in the third quarter is concerning.
Two of the lab values came back concerning enough to repeat.

entries.pronunciation note: no weak form — like the other participial prepositions (regarding, respecting, touching) it keeps its stressed second syllable in every register; only the prefix vowel reduces, to /kən-/
entries.русский: касательно, относительно — офиц. предлог темы; омоним — прилагательное «тревожный»
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, gerund (concerning failing to file on time), or a fused wh-nominal (concerning who authorized the transfer) — never a finite that-clause. ✗ Concerning that he resigned is impossible; write concerning his resignation or concerning the fact that he resigned.
entries.pattern: [clause] concerning [noun phrase] · Concerning [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: Regarding is the neutral business default; concerning is heavier and gravitates toward inquiries, complaints, allegations, and official correspondence. Cross-class test — the object: the preposition always has one and never follows a linking verb (a complaint concerning the instructor), while the modern adjective meaning "worrying" has no object and sits happily after is (that's concerning, a concerning trend). If you can drop very in front of it, you have the adjective.
entries.see also: regarding, respecting, touching, as concerns, about, considering

entries.meaning: Latin for "in the matter of," and used for exactly that. Outside case captions it is affected.
examples: In re Gault remains the foundational juvenile due-process case.
The clerk filed it under In re Estate of Margaret Voss.
In re Marriage of Hoffman was decided the following term.
Counsel cited three bankruptcy opinions, all captioned in re the same debtor.
The docket entry read simply In re Grand Jury Subpoena.
entries.pronunciation note: in-RAY (also in-REE) · no weak form — the re carries the stress and keeps its full vowel, and the Latin in is not the reduced English in of in a minute
entries.русский: юр. по делу, в отношении — лат. «в деле»; в заголовках судебных дел
entries.complement: a noun phrase, almost always a proper name or the name of an estate, matter, or proceeding. No gerund, and no clause of any kind — not a that-clause and not a wh-nominal.
entries.pattern: In re [noun phrase] — as a case caption, docket heading, or file label
entries.variants: sub nom. (short for sub nomine, "under the name of") — the companion caption tag used when the same matter was decided below under a different name; In the Matter of, the English rendering, which some state courts prefer in full
entries.contrast: Re is the clipped commercial descendant of this phrase and belongs in memos, not pleadings. In re survives in American practice mainly to caption a matter that has no opposing party — a bankruptcy, an estate, a juvenile proceeding — where there is no v. to write.
entries.see also: re, in the matter of, in point of, concerning

entries.meaning: Names the business at hand with deliberate ceremony. In running prose it signals that something official is being disposed of.
examples: In the matter of the disputed easement, the court found for the defendant.
The board has reached no conclusion in the matter of the missing funds.
In the matter of your suspension, you may request a hearing within ten days.
She was called to testify in the matter of the 2019 audit.
In the matter of who pays for repairs, the lease is unambiguous.
entries.русский: по делу, по вопросу о — офиц./юр. торжественное обозначение предмета разбирательства
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a fused wh-nominal (in the matter of who pays for repairs); never a finite that-clause (✗ in the matter of that the funds are missing).
entries.pattern: In the matter of [noun phrase] · [clause] in the matter of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The English of in re, and the form you want when you are writing for readers rather than for a docket. Against on the subject of, it is heavier and implies a proceeding, a decision, or a formal position rather than a conversation.
entries.see also: in re, on the subject of, concerning, regarding

entries.meaning: The defamation element that hardened into a preposition. It asks not what a statement was about but whom it pointed at, and a statement about a large enough group points at nobody.
examples: The complaint fails to allege that the broadcast was of and concerning the plaintiff.
A statement of and concerning a group of two hundred employees rarely defames any one of them.
The jury was asked whether the column was of and concerning the sheriff.
Nothing in the review is of and concerning the restaurant's owner personally.
The court held that the caption alone made the article of and concerning her.
Plaintiffs must plead facts showing that the post was of and concerning them.
entries.pronunciation note: uv-und-kun-SUR-ning · both function words at the front reduce almost to nothing — /ə(v) ən/ — and the whole weight of the phrase sits on -cern-
entries.русский: юр. «о и в отношении» — в делах о диффамации: что высказывание указывало именно на истца
entries.register: legal — a term of art in American defamation law, and effectively nonexistent outside it
entries.type: complex (a legal binomial: two near-synonyms coordinated and frozen together)
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a person or an entity, namely the plaintiff. No gerund and no clause of any kind: ✗ of and concerning that he took the money, ✗ of and concerning defaming him. The object is always a who and never a what, which is the sharpest difference between this phrase and ordinary concerning.
entries.pattern: [statement, article, broadcast, publication] of and concerning [the plaintiff] · the statement was of and concerning the plaintiff
entries.contrast: Not an ornamental way of writing about or concerning. It names one element of the tort: a defamation plaintiff must prove that the statement was of and concerning him, meaning an ordinary reader would have understood it to point at him in particular, and a complaint that never pleads the phrase invites a motion to dismiss. Modern drafters cut legal doublets — give, devise and bequeath, null and void — as redundant, but this one has been fixed by a century of case law and cannot be shortened to about without losing the term of art. Where an American meets it: a libel or slander complaint, a motion to dismiss, and the pattern jury instruction read aloud at the end of the trial.
entries.see also: concerning, in re, in the matter of, about, on the part of

entries.meaning: Announces the topic explicitly, either to open it or to change to it.
examples: On the subject of money, we should talk before the meeting.
He has written three books on the subject of memory.
The senator has been notably quiet on the subject of the pipeline.
On the subject of who pays for the venue, nothing has been decided.
She had strong opinions on the subject of letting children lose at games.
On the subject of dinner — is anyone actually cooking?
entries.русский: на тему, по поводу — прямо объявляет тему или переход к ней
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a fused wh-nominal (on the subject of who pays); never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: On the subject of [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] on the subject of [noun phrase]
entries.variants: on the topic of (interchangeable); on the question of (leans toward a matter genuinely in dispute); on the matter of (heavier, and drifting toward in the matter of)
entries.contrast: Fronted, it works like speaking of — a bridge from what was just said. Mid-sentence it is simply an expanded on, and the expansion buys you the ability to attach a long noun phrase without ambiguity: a chapter on the subject of nineteenth-century tariffs cannot be misread the way a chapter on nineteenth-century tariffs occasionally can.
entries.see also: about, on, speaking of, in the matter of, as for

entries.meaning: The preposition of things people quarrel about. Whenever the head noun or verb involves conflict, grief, deliberation, or consequence, English reaches for over rather than about — and the choice is idiomatic rather than logical, so it has to be learned verb by verb.
examples: The strike began as an argument over scheduling software.
Two families have been in court over forty feet of shoreline.
Congress deadlocked over the disaster funding bill.
There is still disagreement over who signs the release.
The deputy director resigned over the handling of the complaint.
The city was sued over the condition of the pumping station.
Two contractors were charged over the falsified inspection reports.
He's still beating himself up over one bad quarter.
She pored over the lease for the better part of an hour.
Nobody is going to cry over a broken plate.
The meeting was over by four.
He handed over the keys without a word.
Come over whenever you like.

senses.head: The matter two parties are fighting about
body: After the nouns argument, dispute, fight, quarrel, row, battle, standoff, litigation, deadlock and the verbs argue, fight, quarrel, clash, split, fall out, deadlock, haggle.
examples: The strike began as an argument over scheduling software.
Two families have been in court over forty feet of shoreline.
Congress deadlocked over the disaster funding bill.
There is still disagreement over who signs the release.

senses.head: The trigger of a strong reaction — a resignation, a lawsuit, an arrest, a firing
examples: The deputy director resigned over the handling of the complaint.
The city was sued over the condition of the pumping station.
Two contractors were charged over the falsified inspection reports.

senses.head: The subject of worry, grief, fuss, or slow deliberation
body: After agonize, brood, fret, fuss, obsess, pore, mull, labor, grieve, cry.
examples: He's still beating himself up over one bad quarter.
She pored over the lease for the better part of an hour.
Nobody is going to cry over a broken plate.

senses.head: Not a preposition — the adverb, adjective, and verb particle
body: No object follows it.
examples: The meeting was over by four.
He handed over the keys without a word.
Come over whenever you like.

entries.pronunciation note: no weak form — unlike the one-syllable prepositions around it, over keeps its stress and its full first vowel even in fast speech; the clipped o'er /ɔr/ is poetic only
entries.русский: из-за, по поводу — предмет спора, реакции, переживаний: argue over — спорить из-за
entries.type: simple — also an adverb and adjective (the meeting was over), a verb particle (hand it over, think it over), and a directional adverb (come over)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, gerund (sued over failing to disclose the defect), or a fused wh-nominal in the dispute sense (a fight over who gets the house, disagreement over whether to appeal) — never a finite that-clause (✗ they argued over that the rent was late → they argued over the late rent). As an adverb or particle it takes no object at all, which is the test that separates the two.
entries.pattern: [noun of conflict] over [noun phrase] · [verb of conflict, distress, or deliberation] over [noun phrase] · over [wh-nominal] · stranded: what exactly are they fighting over?
entries.contrast: Against about, over adds friction: you talk about the merger but you fight over it, and a discussion about the budget and a dispute over the budget differ in temperature, not in subject. Against on, which frames a topic for study, over frames it for combat. Against in connection with, over names the cause outright where that phrase deliberately declines to. Cross-class test — the object: they argued over the bill is the preposition (object the bill); the argument was over is the adjective, with nothing after it; hand it over is a particle, where the object it belongs to hand and over governs nothing; and come over sometime is a bare directional adverb.
entries.senses treated elsewhere: this entry covers only the topic senses. The spatial ("above," "across"), covering, authority, medium, and "more than" senses are in movement and direction; the "spanning a period" sense (over the weekend) is in time.
entries.see also: about, in connection with, on, concerning, over (movement and direction), over (time)

entries.meaning: The subject line of the English language. It labels what a document is about, and it does not belong in the body of one.
examples: Re: Termination of Lease, 41 Colfax Avenue.
The memo was headed Re: Q3 headcount and ran to nine pages.
Re: your voicemail — the shipment left Tuesday.
Please reply to my note re the Thursday deposition.
Every filing in the folder was marked re the same policy number.
He sent one line re the Henderson closing and nothing since.

senses.head: As a heading, followed by a colon
body: The overwhelmingly commoner use, and the only one that is above criticism.
examples: Re: Termination of Lease, 41 Colfax Avenue.
The memo was headed Re: Q3 headcount and ran to nine pages.
Re: your voicemail — the shipment left Tuesday.

senses.head: Inside running text or a file label — jargon, and worth replacing with about or regarding
examples: Please reply to my note re the Thursday deposition.
Every filing in the folder was marked re the same policy number.
He sent one line re the Henderson closing and nothing since.

entries.pronunciation note: REE (also RAY) · no weak form — it is a stressed monosyllable on the rare occasions it is read aloud
entries.русский: по вопросу о, «Тема:» — в шапке письма; внутри текста — канцелярит
entries.register: business and legal shorthand — written only, and effectively never spoken in running prose
entries.type: simple (a clipping of Latin in re)
entries.complement: a noun phrase. No gerund, and no clause of any kind; a pronoun object is possible only in the fixed heading Re: yours of the 14th and is otherwise avoided.
entries.pattern: Re: [noun phrase] — as a memo or letter heading · re [noun phrase] — inside a docket line or file label
entries.contrast: Re is not an abbreviation of regarding or of reference, so it takes no period. In a heading it is conventionally followed by a colon; inside a sentence it looks like jargon, and regarding or about is better. Not to be confused with the prefix re- of rewrite and reissue, which is bound and hyphenated where it is written at all, or with the re of do re mi, which is a different word entirely — the preposition is free-standing and takes neither hyphen nor period.
entries.see also: in re, regarding, with reference to, about

entries.meaning: The neutral formal word for "about." It has no attitude, no implication of complaint, and no legal flavor, which is what makes it the safe default in correspondence.
examples: Regarding your application, we expect to decide by the fifteenth.
I have a question regarding the deductible.
The email said nothing regarding payment.
Several parents have written regarding the change to the bus route.
She was cagey regarding her plans after graduation.
The department has issued no guidance regarding remote work.
Regarding who should attend, that's the director's call.
Regarding what the auditors found, nobody will say anything on the record.

senses.head: Concerning — the plain topic sense
examples: Regarding your application, we expect to decide by the fifteenth.
I have a question regarding the deductible.
The email said nothing regarding payment.

senses.head: Attaching a topic to a noun or adjective of communication
body: After question, silence, guidance, correspondence, and after cagey, evasive, forthcoming, explicit.
examples: Several parents have written regarding the change to the bus route.
She was cagey regarding her plans after graduation.
The department has issued no guidance regarding remote work.

senses.head: With a fused wh-nominal, where the topic is itself an open question
examples: Regarding who should attend, that's the director's call.
Regarding what the auditors found, nobody will say anything on the record.

entries.pronunciation note: no weak form — the stress on -gard- is fixed, and the -ing may go /-ɪn/ in casual speech but the vowel of the stressed syllable never reduces
entries.русский: относительно, по поводу — стандартный деловой предлог темы в амер. английском
entries.register: neutral to formal; the standard word in American business writing
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, gerund (regarding filing after the deadline), or a fused wh-nominal (regarding what the auditors found, regarding whether to appeal) — never a finite that-clause (✗ regarding that the auditors found an error → regarding the auditors' finding).
entries.pattern: [clause] regarding [noun phrase] · Regarding [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: The shortest member of the regard family and the only one that is a single word — prefer it to with regard to, in regard to, and as regards, which say the same thing in three words. There is no s: regardings and as regarding are not English, and regarding to is an error. Cross-class test — the subject: the preposition implies no subject and can open a sentence with nothing to attach to (Regarding your application, a decision is due Friday); the identically spelled present participle of the verb regard must share its subject with the main clause (Regarding the painting closely, she noticed the repair — she is doing the regarding). If the -ing word has an agent, it is the participle.
entries.see also: concerning, with regard to, as regards, respecting, about

entries.meaning: The eighteenth-century sibling of regarding, preserved mostly by constitutional and statutory text.
examples: Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion.
The trustee has broad discretion respecting the sale of estate property.
Rules respecting the admission of new members are set out in Article IV.
He would say nothing respecting the terms of the settlement.
The manual is vague respecting overtime.
Respecting her wishes, the family held no service.
A statute respecting tribal sovereignty may be one that concerns it or one that defers to it, and the sentence will not tell you which.

senses.head: Concerning, about — the prepositional sense
examples: Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion.
The trustee has broad discretion respecting the sale of estate property.
Rules respecting the admission of new members are set out in Article IV.
He would say nothing respecting the terms of the settlement.
The manual is vague respecting overtime.

senses.head: Not a preposition — the present participle of the verb respect, which is the collision that is killing the word
body: The participle has a subject; the preposition does not.
examples: Respecting her wishes, the family held no service.
A statute respecting tribal sovereignty may be one that concerns it or one that defers to it, and the sentence will not tell you which.

entries.pronunciation note: no weak form — identical in this respect to the noun phrase with respect to, where respect also keeps its full stressed vowel while the words around it reduce
entries.русский: устар./юр. относительно, касательно — совпадает с деепричастием «уважая»
entries.register: formal and dated; still productive in legal drafting
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (respecting selling the timber); a fused wh-nominal is grammatical but rare (respecting who may vote); never a finite that-clause (✗ respecting that the trust was funded).
entries.pattern: [clause] respecting [noun phrase] · Respecting [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: The reason this word is fading is that it collides head-on with the participle of the verb respect. A law respecting religion means "a law about religion" in the First Amendment and "a law that shows deference to religion" in ordinary modern reading — and nothing in the sentence disambiguates. Use regarding or about unless you are quoting.
entries.see also: regarding, concerning, touching, with respect to, in respect of

entries.meaning: The Renaissance word for "concerning," now confined to deliberate period style, older legal instruments, and church documents.
examples: Touching the matter of the boundary wall, the parties are agreed.
He left instructions touching the disposal of his library.
Touching your inquiry of the tenth, I can say little.
There is an ancient canon touching the fitness of candidates.
She wrote at length touching her father's debts.
It was a touching tribute, and nobody had expected it.
He read the whole letter without touching the envelope again.

senses.head: Concerning — the prepositional sense
examples: Touching the matter of the boundary wall, the parties are agreed.
He left instructions touching the disposal of his library.
Touching your inquiry of the tenth, I can say little.
There is an ancient canon touching the fitness of candidates.
She wrote at length touching her father's debts.

senses.head: Not a preposition — the adjective meaning "moving" and the participle of the verb touch
body: Neither governs a topic, and the adjective governs nothing at all.
examples: It was a touching tribute, and nobody had expected it.
He read the whole letter without touching the envelope again.

entries.pronunciation note: no weak form — stress falls on the first syllable and stays there
entries.русский: устар./книжн. касательно, относительно — архаичный предлог темы
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund; a fused wh-nominal is possible in older text (touching what was owed him); never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] touching [noun phrase] · Touching [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.variants: touching on, touching upon — these are the living verb-plus-particle construction (the report touches on funding) and are a different structure from the preposition, which needs no on.
entries.contrast: Identical in meaning to concerning and three hundred years older in feel. It also has an unrelated adjective twin meaning "moving" (a touching tribute), so a modern reader hits touching the estate and stalls.
entries.see also: concerning, respecting, anent, regarding

entries.meaning: A survival from Middle English, kept in circulation by Scottish legal usage and by writers reaching for a period effect.
examples: Anent the disposition of the estate, the sheriff has issued no interlocutor.
He wrote a long, cranky letter to the editor anent the new parking scheme.
There is an old rule anent the grazing of sheep on common land.
Anent your question, I have consulted the minutes.
The pamphlet sets out the author's views anent the theater.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form — the stressed second syllable keeps its full vowel and only the unstressed a- reduces
entries.русский: устар. относительно, касательно — шотландский юридический архаизм
entries.register: archaic; alive in Scots law and in deliberately antique or jocular writing
entries.complement: noun phrase only. A gerund is grammatical but unidiomatic, and no clause of any kind will go here — not a that-clause and not a wh-nominal.
entries.pattern: [clause] anent [noun phrase] · Anent [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: Means precisely concerning and adds nothing but age. Readers who do not know it will assume you meant ancient or mistyped something, which is a good reason to leave it alone outside Scotland.
entries.see also: concerning, touching, regarding, in the matter of

entries.meaning: Marks a remark as occasioned by something just mentioned. Its single most common appearance in American English is the fixed phrase apropos of nothing, which announces the opposite — a remark with no connection to anything.
examples: Apropos of your point about staffing, we lost two nurses last month.
She mentioned, apropos of the renovation, that the wiring was original.
Apropos of nothing, my brother once met him in an airport.
He announced, apropos of nothing at all, that he was learning Portuguese.
Her question was brief and entirely apropos.
The timing of the announcement was hardly apropos.

senses.head: Prompted by, arising out of
examples: Apropos of your point about staffing, we lost two nurses last month.
She mentioned, apropos of the renovation, that the wiring was original.

senses.head: The fixed phrase apropos of nothing
examples: Apropos of nothing, my brother once met him in an airport.
He announced, apropos of nothing at all, that he was learning Portuguese.

senses.head: As an adjective — no object, and no of
examples: Her question was brief and entirely apropos.
The timing of the announcement was hardly apropos.

entries.русский: по поводу, в связи с — книжн.; apropos of nothing — «ни с того ни с сего»
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a fused wh-nominal (apropos of what you just said); never a finite that-clause. As an adjective (sense 3) it takes no complement at all.
entries.pattern: Apropos of [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause], apropos of [noun phrase]
entries.variants: à propos of (with the accent; older and now uncommon in American text); bare apropos used directly as a preposition (apropos your email) — widespread, but conservative usage guides still want the of.
entries.contrast: Not a general synonym for about. It means "prompted by" or "arising out of," so it needs something already on the table to arise from. It is also an adjective meaning "apt" (an apropos remark), where it takes no object at all.
entries.see also: speaking of, as for, regarding, vis-à-vis

entries.meaning: Frames a topic in formal writing, usually to mark a shift to one part of a larger question.
examples: As concerns the second charge, the evidence is thin.
The policy is unchanged as concerns part-time employees.
As concerns funding, the department has made no commitment.
Nothing in the agreement is ambiguous as concerns termination.
As concerns what happens after the merger, no one will say.
entries.русский: что касается — офиц. ввод темы, обычно при переходе к её части
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a wh-clause; never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: As concerns [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] as concerns [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Built exactly like as regards, with a verb agreeing with an implied subject, which is why the -s is fixed: as concern is an error, and there is no as concerns to. Rarer and stiffer than as regards; regarding beats both.
entries.see also: as regards, concerning, as for, as to

entries.meaning: The drafter's pointer. It ties a term to the place where its meaning is fixed, so the meaning never has to be written twice — and so that amending it once amends it everywhere.
examples: "Confidential Information," as defined in Section 1.2, survives termination of this Agreement.
The tenant is a small business as defined in the Small Business Act.
Benefits vest on a Change of Control as defined in the Plan and on no other event.
Overtime is computed on the regular rate as defined in the Fair Labor Standards Act.
The policy excludes flood as defined in the National Flood Insurance Program.
Each capitalized term not otherwise defined here has the meaning given it as defined in the master agreement.
entries.pronunciation note: az-dih-FYND-in · the stress is on -fined; as and final in both reduce, and in fast reading the whole phrase runs together as /əzdəˈfaɪndɪn/
entries.русский: юр. в значении, определённом в — отсылка к месту, где термин определён
entries.type: complex and participial — a reduced passive clause (as [it is] defined in) hardened into a cross-reference marker
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a text: a section, subsection, article, exhibit, schedule, statute, rule, or the agreement itself (as defined in Section 1.2, as defined in the Plan). No gerund and no clause of any kind — ✗ as defined in that the parties agreed, ✗ as defined in setting the price. Where the text being pointed at is the present one, American drafters switch to an adverb that governs nothing: as defined herein, as defined above.
entries.pattern: [defined term, capitalized or in quotation marks] as defined in [text reference] · "Change of Control," as defined in Section 8(c), ...
entries.variants: as defined herein, as defined above, as defined below (adverbs, no object); as that term is defined in (the unhurried long form); as defined by, which takes an agent rather than a place — as defined by the Secretary names who did the defining, not where the definition sits
entries.contrast: Three drafting phrases do three different jobs and are mixed constantly. As defined in points at where a meaning lives; within the meaning of asserts that a thing falls inside that meaning; and as used in writes the meaning down. So: an "affiliate" as defined in Rule 12b-2 (the definition is over there), an affiliate within the meaning of Rule 12b-2 (this company is one), and as used in this Act, "affiliate" means (here is the definition). Where an American meets it: a lease, an employment agreement, an insurance policy, a 401(k) summary, and every filing the company makes with the SEC.
entries.see also: as used in, within the meaning of, as set forth in, as provided in, for purposes of

entries.meaning: The English topic-switch marker. It picks one item out of a set under discussion and turns to it.
examples: The tomatoes did well. As for the peppers, something ate them.
As for me, I'd rather drive.
She got a raise and a corner office. As for her old team, they were reassigned.
As for paying the whole thing up front, that isn't happening.
The engine is fine. As for the transmission, I'd get a second opinion.
As for what he said afterward, I'd rather not repeat it.
entries.русский: что касается, а вот — переключение темы: выбирает один пункт из обсуждаемых
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun (as for me, as for them — never as for I), gerund, or a fused wh-nominal (as for what he said afterward); ✗ never a finite that-clause (✗ as for that he was late).
entries.pattern: As for [noun phrase], [clause]. — essentially always sentence-initial; it cannot be stranded and it does not sit comfortably at the end of a sentence.
entries.contrast: As for switches to a topic already in play, usually one of several items, and very often signals that the new item will fare worse than the last (As for the rest of you...). As to raises a matter for consideration and can sit anywhere in the sentence. With regard to and as regards are neutral framing devices with no contrastive charge at all.
entries.see also: as to, as regards, speaking of, as far as X is concerned, on the subject of

entries.meaning: The invoice-and-work-order preposition. It survives because it sounds official, and it survives in spite of a century of hostility from every American usage authority that has bothered to mention it.
examples: As per your instructions, the shipment was split across two pallets.
The invoice was issued as per the terms of the master agreement.
Overtime is calculated as per Section 14 of the handbook.
As per our conversation Tuesday, I've attached the revised scope.
The samples were stored as per the manufacturer's specification.
He showed up twenty minutes late, as per usual.
The printer jammed on the first page, as per usual.

senses.head: In accordance with a stated instruction, document, or standard
body: The object is the thing that was followed.
examples: As per your instructions, the shipment was split across two pallets.
The invoice was issued as per the terms of the master agreement.
Overtime is calculated as per Section 14 of the handbook.
As per our conversation Tuesday, I've attached the revised scope.
The samples were stored as per the manufacturer's specification.

senses.head: The fixed phrase as per usual
body: Jocular or dialectal, and not a use of sense 1 — nothing is being conformed to.
examples: He showed up twenty minutes late, as per usual.
The printer jammed on the first page, as per usual.

entries.русский: согласно, в соответствии с — коммерч.; as per usual — шутл. «как обычно»
entries.register: business and commercial; long and loudly disliked by usage guides
entries.type: complex (English as + Latin per "through, by," pressed into commercial service)
entries.complement: noun phrase only — a document, an instruction, a conversation, or a published standard. No gerund, no wh-nominal, and never a finite clause: ✗ as per you asked → as per your request, or better, as you asked.
entries.pattern: As per [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] as per [noun phrase] · fixed: as per usual
entries.variants: bare per (per your email, per the contract) — shorter, and now the commoner form in American business writing; as per usual, a jocular or dialectal substitute for as usual
entries.contrast: As per claims conformity with a prior instruction, which is what separates it from the rest of this family: in reference to and with reference to merely name a document, while as per asserts that the document was followed. It is redundant on its face — per by itself already means "in accordance with" — which is why editors reduce it to per, under, following, or as you asked. Do not confuse it with distributive per (sixty miles per hour, twelve dollars per person), which is a different word doing arithmetic and is perfectly respectable.
entries.see also: according to, in reference to, with reference to, in accordance with, as regards

entries.meaning: The drafter's cross-reference to a governing rule. It borrows the authority of a named provision instead of restating it, and the except frame in front of it is doing most of the work in American statutes.
examples: Except as provided in subsection (b), no permit may be issued after June 30.
Notice shall be given as provided in Article 9 of the bylaws.
The deposit is refundable as provided in the lease and not otherwise.
Interest accrues as provided in Section 4.3.
As provided in the settlement, payments begin thirty days after entry of judgment.
Coverage terminates as provided in the plan document, whatever the enrollment portal says.
entries.pronunciation note: az-pruh-VY-did-in · four syllables of which only -vy- is stressed, so the phrase is easy to miss in read-aloud statutory language
entries.русский: юр. как предусмотрено в — отсылка к норме вместо её повторения
entries.register: legal and statutory; the standard American drafting connective
entries.type: complex and participial — a reduced passive clause (as [it is] provided in)
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a text — a section, subsection, article, rule, statute, or instrument. No gerund and no clause of any kind (✗ as provided in that notice is given). The sibling as provided by takes an agent or a body of law instead (as provided by law, as provided by the Secretary), and as provided herein substitutes an adverb and governs nothing.
entries.pattern: Except as provided in [text], [rule] · [rule], as provided in [text] · As provided in [text], [clause]
entries.variants: except as provided in — much the commonest frame, and the one that carves an exception out of a rule the sentence has just stated; as otherwise provided in; as provided by law; as provided herein (adverb, no object)
entries.contrast: As set forth in points at where something is written out; as provided in points at where something is directed, so its object is a rule that governs rather than a description that informs. Against pursuant to, which says an act was taken under a named authority, this phrase says the manner, the timing, or the exception is stated in it — notice given pursuant to Article 9 was authorized by Article 9, while notice given as provided in Article 9 followed the recipe there. Where an American meets it: a statute, a municipal code, a set of bylaws, a lease, and any notice arriving from a state agency.
entries.see also: as set forth in, as defined in, as per, pursuant to, in accordance with

entries.meaning: A formal, slightly British-flavored way to introduce a topic. Every American editor will shorten it to regarding or about.
examples: As regards the deposit, the tenant has thirty days to dispute it.
The rules are stricter as regards imported produce.
As regards staffing, nothing changes until January.
He was evasive as regards the source of the funds.
As regards whether the flight is refundable, read the fare rules.
entries.русский: что касается — офиц.; амер. редактор заменит на regarding или about
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a wh-clause; never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: As regards [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] as regards [noun phrase]
entries.variants: as respects (rare, and now chiefly American insurance drafting)
entries.contrast: As regards to is an error — a blend of as regards and with regard to. Choose one or the other. And note that this is the one place in the family where an s is correct: regards here is the verb regard agreeing with an implied subject ("as it regards"), not the plural of the noun. Compare with regard to, where the s is always wrong.
entries.see also: with regard to, in regard to, as concerns, regarding, as for

entries.meaning: The rarest of the three as-plus-verb frames. An American is most likely to meet it on the declarations page or an endorsement of an insurance policy, where it restricts a limit, a deductible, or an exclusion to one slice of the coverage.
examples: The limit applies separately as respects each insured location.
As respects bodily injury, the deductible is waived.
This insurance is excess as respects any other valid and collectible coverage.
The policy is silent as respects mold.
As respects the second count, the demurrer is sustained.
Nothing in the endorsement changes the policy as respects property damage.
entries.pronunciation note: az-rih-SPEKTS · the final cluster /kts/ is regularly simplified to /ks/ in speech, which is one reason the phrase is so rarely said aloud
entries.русский: офиц./устар. в отношении — живёт в амер. страховых полисах: сужает условие до части покрытия
entries.register: formal and legal, and now decidedly dated; its one living home is American insurance drafting
entries.type: complex — a fossilized clause whose verb agrees with an unexpressed subject ("as it respects")
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (as respects filing after the deadline); a fused wh-nominal is grammatical but vanishingly rare; never a finite that-clause (✗ as respects that the loss occurred in June).
entries.pattern: As respects [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] as respects [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Built exactly like as regards and as concerns, and the -s is fixed for the same reason: it is verb agreement, not a plural noun. As respect is an error and so is as respects to. Do not confuse it with with respect to, the standard American phrase, or with in respect of, the British one, and keep it clear of out of respect for, which is about deference rather than topic. On a policy declarations page it does real work, fencing a limit to one coverage part; in ordinary prose it is an antique, and regarding is the repair.
entries.see also: as regards, as concerns, with respect to, in respect of, regarding

entries.meaning: The drafter's pointer to content stated somewhere else in the same instrument. It says the words are over there and spares the reader a second copy of them.
examples: The vendor shall perform the services as set forth in Exhibit A.
Compensation is as set forth in Schedule 2 and may not be changed orally.
The parties acknowledge the recitals as set forth in the preamble.
Payment terms are as set forth in the purchase order.
As set forth in the court's earlier opinion, the statute has no retroactive effect.
Milestones are as more particularly set forth in the statement of work.
entries.pronunciation note: az-set-FORTH-in · the stress lands on forth, and set is unstressed enough that many speakers reduce its vowel to /ə/
entries.русский: юр. как изложено в — отсылка к тексту в том же документе
entries.register: legal and contractual; the workhorse cross-reference of American drafting
entries.type: complex and participial — a reduced passive clause built on the phrasal verb set forth
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a text or a place inside one — Exhibit A, Schedule 2, the recitals, Section 4, the attached specification. No gerund and no clause of any kind (✗ as set forth in that the parties agreed). As set forth herein, above, and below substitute an adverb and govern nothing.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] as set forth in [text] · on the terms set forth in [text] · as more particularly set forth in [text]
entries.variants: as set out in (British and Commonwealth); as described in, as specified in, as stated in (plainer, and better anywhere outside a contract); as set forth herein / above / below (adverbs, no object); as more fully set forth in and as more particularly set forth in (the drafter's emphatic forms)
entries.contrast: Against as defined in, which points at a meaning, and as provided in, which points at a rule, this phrase points at content — the place where something is written out in full. It is also the member of the three that most readily decays into padding: the services set forth in Exhibit A is doing work, while as set forth in this Agreement above is doing none, and an editor will cut it. Note the vocabulary trap: set forth here is the old sense "state, lay out," not the sense of setting forth on a journey.
entries.see also: as defined in, as provided in, as used in, as per, in accordance with

entries.meaning: The standard bridge from a noun of uncertainty to an indirect question. That is the job it does that no other member of this family does as cleanly.
examples: There is real doubt as to whether the roof will last the winter.
She gave no hint as to where she'd been.
The report reaches no conclusion as to who ordered the transfer.
The manual gives no guidance as to how to reset the controller.
The parties remain apart as to damages.
He was questioned as to his whereabouts on the night of the fire.
The lease says nothing as to subletting the garage.
As to the second proposal, the board took no action.
As to money, we'll discuss that when the work is done.

senses.head: Attaching a wh- or whether-clause to a noun of doubt, question, or dispute
examples: There is real doubt as to whether the roof will last the winter.
She gave no hint as to where she'd been.
The report reaches no conclusion as to who ordered the transfer.
The manual gives no guidance as to how to reset the controller.

senses.head: Concerning, with an ordinary noun phrase or a gerund
examples: The parties remain apart as to damages.
He was questioned as to his whereabouts on the night of the fire.
The lease says nothing as to subletting the garage.

senses.head: Fronted, as a topic marker — an older use, now overlapping with as for
examples: As to the second proposal, the board took no action.
As to money, we'll discuss that when the work is done.

entries.русский: относительно, насчёт — вводит косвенный вопрос: as to whether — «относительно того, ...ли»
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (as to paying the balance), or a wh-clause ✗ including one headed by whether (as to whether the deal closes) — ✗ never a finite that-clause (✗ no doubt as to that the roof will fail) and never a bare infinitive (✗ as to pay the balance). The to here is a preposition, which is why a verb after it takes -ing; the one construction that looks like an exception is the infinitival indirect question, where the infinitive belongs to the wh-word and not to as to: no guidance as to how to proceed, undecided as to whether to appeal.
entries.pattern: [noun of doubt or dispute] as to [wh-clause] · [clause] as to [noun phrase] · As to [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: After a verb, as to is usually deadweight: they disagreed as to how it happened is better as they disagreed about how it happened. After an abstract noun it earns its place, because bare of would change the meaning or fail outright — no evidence as to motive is standard, questions as to whether is standard, and doubt of whether is not English. Against as for, as to does not switch topics; it opens a question.
entries.see also: as for, as regards, with regard to, in relation to, about

entries.meaning: The phrase that opens a definitions section. It announces that the meanings about to be given are local, and that the ordinary English senses of those same words are left undisturbed everywhere else.
examples: As used in this chapter, "vehicle" includes a trailer.
As used in the ordinance, "night" means the hours between ten and six.
As used in this Agreement, "Business Day" excludes federal holidays.
As used in Title VII, "employer" reaches any entity with fifteen or more employees.
As used in these regulations, the singular includes the plural.
The word carries its ordinary meaning except as used in subsection (d).
entries.pronunciation note: az-YOOZD-in · note the /z/ and the voiced ending: used here is the passive participle of use, so it is /juzd/, and it is never the /just/ of used to
entries.русский: юр. в значении, используемом в — открывает раздел определений: значение только для этого текста
entries.register: legal and statutory; the standard American opener of a definitions section
entries.type: complex and participial — a reduced passive clause (as [it is] used in)
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the text whose vocabulary is being fenced — this section, this chapter, this Act, these regulations, this Agreement. No gerund and no clause of any kind (✗ as used in that the statute says). The object is always the text, never the term: ✗ as used in "employee" is impossible, because the term belongs in the subject of what follows.
entries.pattern: As used in [text], [term] means [definition] · As used in [text], the following terms have the following meanings
entries.contrast: The mirror image of as defined in. As used in stands at the head of the definition and creates the local meaning; as defined in stands beside the term somewhere else and borrows it. Against for purposes of, which fences any rule — substantive or definitional — to a named body of law, this phrase fences the vocabulary alone, and in the definitional case the two are near-interchangeable: as used in this section, "resident" means and for purposes of this section, "resident" means differ only in house style. Where an American meets it: the first paragraph of almost any statute, ordinance, or regulation, and the definitions article of any contract long enough to have one.
entries.see also: as defined in, for purposes of, within the meaning of, as set forth in, in the matter of

entries.meaning: States that something is linked to a matter without specifying how. That vagueness is the point, both in journalism and in contracts.
examples: Two men were detained in connection with the warehouse fire.
She was interviewed in connection with an ongoing investigation.
No charges have been filed in connection with the incident.
The firm disclosed fees paid in connection with the offering.
All expenses incurred in connection with relocating will be reimbursed.
The indemnity covers any claim in connection with the services.
He resigned in connection with the audit findings, though the company said otherwise.
Two supervisors were reassigned in connection with the missing inventory.

senses.head: Linked to an event, with no claim about how — the police department's and the reporter's hedge
examples: Two men were detained in connection with the warehouse fire.
She was interviewed in connection with an ongoing investigation.
No charges have been filed in connection with the incident.

senses.head: Arising out of or in the course of a transaction — the drafter's catch-all
body: In contracts and securities filings the breadth is deliberate, so that nothing touching the deal escapes the clause.
examples: The firm disclosed fees paid in connection with the offering.
All expenses incurred in connection with relocating will be reimbursed.
The indemnity covers any claim in connection with the services.

senses.head: Loosely causal, where the writer declines to say "because of."
examples: He resigned in connection with the audit findings, though the company said otherwise.
Two supervisors were reassigned in connection with the missing inventory.

entries.русский: в связи с — офиц.: связь с событием без уточнения какая (arrested in connection with)
entries.register: formal; a fixture of police statements, journalism, and securities filings
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (in connection with relocating), or a fused wh-nominal (in connection with what happened that night); never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in connection with [noun phrase] · In connection with [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: In crime reporting this is a deliberate hedge — arrested in connection with the robbery asserts a link without asserting guilt, which arrested for the robbery would. Do not treat the two as interchangeable; the substitution is a defamation problem, not a style choice.
entries.see also: in relation to, over, regarding, with respect to

entries.meaning: Points back to a document, a message, or a prior communication. It is at its most natural when there really is a document being referred to.
examples: In reference to your letter of June 2, the policy lapsed in April.
I'm calling in reference to an invoice we received twice.
The clause is ambiguous in reference to renewal.
In reference to the earlier discussion, the figures have since changed.
She said nothing in reference to the missed deadline.
entries.русский: в связи с, со ссылкой на — деловая переписка: отсылка к письму или документу
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a fused wh-nominal (in reference to what you asked on Tuesday); never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: In reference to [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] in reference to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: With reference to is the commoner of the pair in American business writing and means exactly the same thing. Neither takes an s — in references to is a different construction entirely (plural mentions), and in regards to is the analogous error one family over. Both are stiff; regarding or about is nearly always better.
entries.see also: with reference to, re, regarding, in regard to

entries.meaning: A three-word about, indistinguishable in meaning from with regard to.
examples: In regard to your question, the deadline has not moved.
The two departments have different policies in regard to travel.
In regard to the second invoice, we've issued a credit.
He had no authority in regard to hiring.
Nothing has been decided in regard to next year's budget.
entries.русский: относительно, что касается — офиц. трёхсловное about; то же, что with regard to
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a fused wh-nominal (in regard to who signs the checks); never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: In regard to [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] in regard to [noun phrase]
entries.variants: with regard to — the same phrase with a different opening preposition, and slightly more common in American prose.
entries.contrast: In regards to is an error, and it is one of the most frequent in American office email. The noun is regard, singular. See with regard to for the full rule and the one exception.
entries.see also: with regard to, as regards, regarding, in reference to

examples: The committee has no jurisdiction in relation to private employers.
In relation to the shipping delay, we've waived the fee.
The report says nothing in relation to who approved the overtime.
The engine is enormous in relation to the size of the boat.
Wages have barely moved in relation to rent.
Their sample is tiny in relation to the population they claim to describe.
The debt looks manageable in relation to the company's cash on hand.

senses.head: Concerning, with respect to
examples: The committee has no jurisdiction in relation to private employers.
In relation to the shipping delay, we've waived the fee.
The report says nothing in relation to who approved the overtime.

senses.head: Compared with, measured against, in proportion to
body: The object here must be a noun phrase.
examples: The engine is enormous in relation to the size of the boat.
Wages have barely moved in relation to rent.
Their sample is tiny in relation to the population they claim to describe.
The debt looks manageable in relation to the company's cash on hand.

entries.русский: относительно, в отношении — тема; также «по сравнению с, соразмерно с»
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a fused wh-nominal (in relation to what the policy covers); never a finite that-clause. In the comparative sense (2) the object must be a noun phrase — a gerund will not go there.
entries.pattern: [clause] in relation to [noun phrase] · In relation to [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: The only member of this family that also carries a genuine comparative sense — small in relation to the whole measures one thing against another, which with regard to and as regards cannot do. When you mean nothing but "about," the shorter word is better; when you mean "measured against," this is the right phrase and vis-à-vis is its fancier twin.
entries.see also: vis-à-vis, with respect to, in connection with, in terms of

entries.meaning: Identifies the thing a right, payment, liability, or rule applies to.
examples: No claim may be made in respect of damage caused by ordinary wear.
The company accepted liability in respect of the two damaged pallets.
Nothing is owed in respect of the canceled order.
Tax is payable in respect of the year ending April 5.
A premium is charged in respect of each insured vehicle.
In respect of the remaining units, completion is scheduled for June.
The policy is silent in respect of flood.

senses.head: The subject a right, claim, payment, or liability attaches to
examples: No claim may be made in respect of damage caused by ordinary wear.
The company accepted liability in respect of the two damaged pallets.
Nothing is owed in respect of the canceled order.

senses.head: The period or unit a charge is computed for
body: The tax-and-insurance use, and the one with no short American equivalent — for is usually the answer.
examples: Tax is payable in respect of the year ending April 5.
A premium is charged in respect of each insured vehicle.

senses.head: Concerning, as regards — the plain topic use, which American writers should render with respect to
examples: In respect of the remaining units, completion is scheduled for June.
The policy is silent in respect of flood.

entries.русский: брит./юр. в отношении, по — предмет права, платежа, обязательства; амер. норма — with respect to
entries.register: formal and legal; British and Commonwealth-leaning
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund; never a finite clause of any kind. In its home register — insurance, tax, and contract drafting — the object is almost always a bare noun naming a liability, a period, an asset, or a class of loss.
entries.pattern: [clause] in respect of [noun phrase] · In respect of [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.variants: in respect to (American, but far less common than with respect to); with respect to (the standard American form)
entries.contrast: American writers should use with respect to. In respect of reads as British or as consciously legal, and it is the form that turns up in insurance policies, tax notices, and contracts drafted outside the United States. Do not confuse either with out of respect for, which is about deference, not topic.
entries.see also: with respect to, respecting, in relation to, with regard to

entries.meaning: Restricts a judgment to one dimension, the way as regards does, with a Victorian accent. Modern American writing keeps the anaphoric form and drops the rest.
examples: The proposal was rejected on the score of cost alone.
Nobody has complained on the score of noise.
On the score of safety, the older design is the better one.
He was excused on the score of ill health.
The building is admired on the score of proportion rather than ornament.
The financing is settled; you needn't worry on that score.
entries.русский: устар. по причине, в отношении — живо лишь оборотом on that score «на этот счёт»
entries.register: formal and dated; only the fixed on that score is still ordinary American English
entries.complement: a noun phrase, characteristically a bare abstract noun naming a dimension of judgment — cost, safety, health, taste, proportion. A gerund is grammatical but stiff (on the score of having failed to file), and no clause of any kind will go here.
entries.pattern: [clause] on the score of [noun phrase] · On the score of [noun phrase], [clause] · fixed: on that score, on this score
entries.variants: on that score and on this score — anaphoric, fully alive, and the only forms most Americans ever write (you can set your mind at rest on that score)
entries.contrast: Two readings sit inside the phrase, and they belong to different files. As a topic limiter it means "as regards" — no complaints on the score of comfort — and as a reason phrase it means "on the grounds of," where it overlaps on the grounds of and on account of. The test is what the object names: a dimension gives you the topic sense, a motive the causal one. Nothing to do with music or with keeping score in a game, though the metaphor did start as a tally scratched on a tavern beam.
entries.see also: as regards, in point of, in the way of, on the grounds of, with respect to

examples: The dollar has weakened vis-à-vis the euro.
Our costs are high vis-à-vis the rest of the industry.
Nobody has explained the university's position vis-à-vis the union.
I have questions vis-à-vis the payment schedule.
Vis-à-vis the hiring freeze, no exceptions are being granted.
He found himself vis-à-vis the one person he'd hoped to avoid.
The two delegations sat vis-à-vis one another at a table the length of the room.

senses.head: In relation to, compared with — the dominant modern sense
examples: The dollar has weakened vis-à-vis the euro.
Our costs are high vis-à-vis the rest of the industry.
Nobody has explained the university's position vis-à-vis the union.

senses.head: Concerning, with regard to
examples: I have questions vis-à-vis the payment schedule.
Vis-à-vis the hiring freeze, no exceptions are being granted.

senses.head: Face to face with — the literal, now rare
examples: He found himself vis-à-vis the one person he'd hoped to avoid.
The two delegations sat vis-à-vis one another at a table the length of the room.

entries.pronunciation note: veez-ah-VEE (both s letters silent) · no weak form — the French stress on the final syllable is kept, and the middle à is already as reduced as it gets
entries.русский: по отношению к, в сравнении с — книжн.; также «относительно» и устар. «лицом к лицу с»
entries.complement: noun phrase; a gerund is possible but stiff (vis-à-vis raising the cap); never a clause of any kind.
entries.pattern: [clause] vis-à-vis [noun phrase] · Vis-à-vis [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.variants: vis-a-vis and vis à vis — the grave accent is optional in American text, the hyphens are standard. All three are pronounced the same.
entries.contrast: Not a synonym for versus. Versus sets two things against each other; vis-à-vis positions one relative to the other without any implication of conflict. Against in relation to, it is shorter, more clearly comparative, and noticeably more self-conscious.
entries.see also: in relation to, with respect to, as regards, apropos of

entries.meaning: Opens a letter or a paragraph by naming the document being answered.
examples: With reference to your email of the eleventh, the parts are on back order.
With reference to the earlier complaint, the account has been credited.
He declined to comment with reference to the pending case.
The drawings are dimensioned with reference to the northeast corner of the slab.
Salaries are set with reference to a published pay band.
Elevations on the survey are given with reference to mean sea level.

senses.head: Naming the document, message, or matter being answered
body: The correspondence use, and the padded one.
examples: With reference to your email of the eleventh, the parts are on back order.
With reference to the earlier complaint, the account has been credited.
He declined to comment with reference to the pending case.

senses.head: Technical: measured, dimensioned, or set against a stated baseline
body: Here it is not padding, and no shorter phrase does the job — this is the sense that overlaps with respect to.
examples: The drawings are dimensioned with reference to the northeast corner of the slab.
Salaries are set with reference to a published pay band.
Elevations on the survey are given with reference to mean sea level.

entries.русский: со ссылкой на, применительно к — в переписке; в технике — «относительно» точки отсчёта
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a fused wh-nominal (with reference to what the drawings show); never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: With reference to [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] with reference to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Interchangeable with in reference to, and marginally more common in American use. In technical writing it shades toward "measured against a stated baseline," which is where it overlaps with with respect to. As with the whole family, no s — with references to means something else.
entries.see also: in reference to, with respect to, with regard to, re

entries.meaning: The most common of the long-form topic phrases, and the one whose plural error is most worth learning to avoid. Note that the negative form is genuinely useful in a way the positive one is not: without regard to means "ignoring," and no single word replaces it.
examples: With regard to the security deposit, we'll need photographs.
The manual says nothing with regard to remote work.
With regard to your second question, the answer is no.
She wrote a careful memo with regard to the licensing terms.
With regard to funding, the grant covers only the first year.
Applicants are ranked without regard to age or ZIP code.
He acted without regard to the consequences.
The formula applies without regard to how long the employee has been there.

senses.head: Concerning — the plain topic sense, and the padded one
body: An editor will cut it to about, to on, or to nothing.
examples: With regard to the security deposit, we'll need photographs.
The manual says nothing with regard to remote work.
With regard to your second question, the answer is no.
She wrote a careful memo with regard to the licensing terms.
With regard to funding, the grant covers only the first year.

senses.head: Negated as without regard to — "ignoring," "leaving out of account."
body: This is the form worth keeping: no single English word replaces it, and it is the standard phrasing in nondiscrimination clauses.
examples: Applicants are ranked without regard to age or ZIP code.
He acted without regard to the consequences.
The formula applies without regard to how long the employee has been there.

entries.русский: относительно, что касается — офиц. многословное about; without regard to — «независимо от»
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (with regard to filing late — the to is a preposition, so with regard to file late is impossible); ✗ never a finite that-clause (✗ with regard to that the rent is late). A fused wh- or whether-nominal is grammatical but clumsy here — write as to whether the deal closes, not with regard to whether the deal closes, and see as to.
entries.pattern: With regard to [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] with regard to [noun phrase] · negated as without regard to [noun phrase]
entries.variants: in regard to; having regard to (legal and British); as regards and regarding as one-word and two-word alternatives
entries.contrast: The singular is the rule: with regard to, in regard to, without regard to. With regards to and in regards to are errors. Regards with an s is the plural of the noun meaning "good wishes" — which is exactly why Best regards closes a letter and give her my regards is idiomatic, while with regards to your invoice is not. The single exception in the whole family is as regards, where regards is a verb, not a noun.
entries.see also: in regard to, as regards, regarding, with respect to, with reference to

examples: With respect to the third count, the jury could not agree.
The lease is silent with respect to subletting.
Company policy with respect to overtime changed in March.
Differentiate the function with respect to x.
The bracket's position is fixed with respect to the frame, not the wheel.
Returns are reported with respect to a benchmark index.

senses.head: Concerning, as regards
examples: With respect to the third count, the jury could not agree.
The lease is silent with respect to subletting.
Company policy with respect to overtime changed in March.

senses.head: Technical: measured or varied against a stated variable or baseline
examples: Differentiate the function with respect to x.
The bracket's position is fixed with respect to the frame, not the wheel.
Returns are reported with respect to a benchmark index.

entries.русский: в отношении, относительно — норма юр. и тех. прозы; в математике — «по» (производная по x)
entries.register: formal; the default in legal, mathematical, and engineering prose
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a fused wh-nominal (with respect to whether the clause survives closing); never a finite that-clause. In the technical sense (2) the object must be a noun phrase naming a variable or a baseline.
entries.pattern: [clause] with respect to [noun phrase] · With respect to [noun phrase], [clause] · abbreviated w.r.t. in technical notation
entries.contrast: With all due respect is a different animal entirely — a discourse hedge announcing that disagreement is coming, not a preposition of topic. And in respect of is the British counterpart of sense 1; American writers should stay with with respect to.
entries.see also: in respect of, with regard to, in relation to, in terms of, respecting

entries.meaning: Says which order of consideration a statement belongs to. In American legal writing it is doing real work; everywhere else it is usually a way of sounding deliberate.
examples: As a matter of law, the release bars every claim in the complaint.
He refused as a matter of principle, knowing it would cost him the contract.
The court reached the question as a matter of first impression.
The company does not comment on personnel decisions as a matter of policy.
Invoices over ten thousand dollars are reviewed twice as a matter of course.
Exit interviews are recorded as a matter of routine.
As a matter of fact, the inspection had already been scheduled.
She wasn't late; as a matter of fact she was the first one there.

senses.head: Restricting a claim to one order of consideration — legal, factual, or principled
examples: As a matter of law, the release bars every claim in the complaint.
He refused as a matter of principle, knowing it would cost him the contract.
The court reached the question as a matter of first impression.

senses.head: Naming a settled practice rather than a decision — as a matter of policy, as a matter of course
examples: The company does not comment on personnel decisions as a matter of policy.
Invoices over ten thousand dollars are reviewed twice as a matter of course.
Exit interviews are recorded as a matter of routine.

senses.head: As a matter of fact — no longer a restriction at all, but a corrective discourse marker
examples: As a matter of fact, the inspection had already been scheduled.
She wasn't late; as a matter of fact she was the first one there.

entries.русский: с точки зрения, в порядке — as a matter of law «юридически»; as a matter of fact «на самом деле»
entries.register: formal; standard in legal, policy, and business prose
entries.complement: a bare abstract noun with no article — law, fact, policy, principle, right, course, practice, convenience. Nothing else goes here: no gerund, no concrete noun, and no clause of any kind (✗ as a matter of the policy, ✗ as a matter of that it was late).
entries.pattern: As a matter of [bare abstract noun], [clause] · [clause] as a matter of [bare abstract noun]
entries.variants: as a matter of course (routinely, without a decision being made each time); as a matter of fact (a discourse marker meaning "actually"); as a matter of law (a term of art: decided by the judge on the legal rule, not by the jury on the evidence)
entries.contrast: The articles are the trap and they run in opposite directions: a is fixed before matter and nothing may stand before the noun after of — as a matter of policy, never ✗ as matter of policy and never ✗ as a matter of the policy. Two of the fixed phrases have drifted apart in meaning: as a matter of law still restricts a claim to one dimension and is the near twin of in point of law, while as a matter of fact has stopped restricting anything and now just means "actually," usually introducing a correction. Against in terms of, which names the units something is measured in, this phrase names the kind of consideration at work — legal, factual, principled, or merely habitual.
entries.see also: in point of, in terms of, for purposes of, with respect to, as far as X is concerned

entries.term: as far as X is concerned
entries.meaning: Restricts a claim to one domain or one person's view, almost always implying that the picture changes outside it.
examples: As far as I'm concerned, the matter is closed.
As far as the wiring is concerned, the inspector found nothing wrong.
The car's fine as far as the engine goes — the body is another story.
As far as the numbers are concerned, we're ahead of last quarter.
As far as she was concerned, the apology had never happened.
As far as scheduling goes, Tuesday is the only day that works.
entries.русский: что касается X — разрывный оборот: объект стоит внутри; намёк, что в другом иначе
entries.type: complex and discontinuous — a fossilized clause that works as a preposition, with its object sitting inside the frame rather than after it
entries.complement: a noun phrase or objective pronoun in the gap (as far as the wiring is concerned); the frame then closes with is/are concerned or goes/go. Never a finite that-clause inside the gap, and note the cross-class trap: as far as followed by a whole clause and no closing is concerned (as far as I know, as far as I can tell, as far as anyone remembers) is the conjunction, a different construction that hedges the speaker's certainty rather than restricting a domain.
entries.pattern: As far as [noun phrase] is concerned, [clause] · [clause], as far as [noun phrase] goes · As far as [pronoun] is concerned, [clause]
entries.variants: as far as X goes (more casual); so far as X is concerned (formal and slightly British); truncated as far as X (As far as money, we're fine) — very common in American speech and still flagged as nonstandard in edited prose.
