entries.contrast: Two different jobs hide in the same frame. With a person as the object it means "in that person's opinion" (as far as I'm concerned, the matter is closed); with a thing it means "within that domain" (as far as the wiring is concerned, the house is fine). Note that the verb agrees with the object: as far as the numbers are concerned.
entries.see also: as for, in terms of, in the way of, with respect to

examples: By way of explanation, he pointed to the schedule on the wall.
She sent flowers by way of apology.
By way of introduction, let me say how the panel will run.
We drove to Santa Fe by way of Taos.
The shipment came by way of Rotterdam.
The prosecution offered little by way of physical evidence.
There isn't much by way of nightlife within thirty miles.

senses.head: As a form of, in the character of, for the purpose of — a bare abstract noun follows
examples: By way of explanation, he pointed to the schedule on the wall.
She sent flowers by way of apology.
By way of introduction, let me say how the panel will run.

senses.head: Via, by the route of — spatial, and treated with the prepositions of path
examples: We drove to Santa Fe by way of Taos.
The shipment came by way of Rotterdam.

senses.head: In the way of, as regards — chiefly in negative or quantified statements
examples: The prosecution offered little by way of physical evidence.
There isn't much by way of nightlife within thirty miles.

entries.русский: в качестве, в порядке — by way of apology «в качестве извинения»; также «через» о маршруте
entries.complement: in sense 1 a bare abstract noun with no article (by way of apology) or a gerund (by way of explaining himself); in senses 2 and 3 an ordinary noun phrase. Never a clause of any kind.
entries.pattern: [clause] by way of [noun phrase] · By way of [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: In the sense that belongs to this file, the object is a bare abstract noun with no article: by way of apology, not by way of an apology. Put an article in and you have either the route sense or a mistake. The route sense (flew to Lisbon by way of Newark) belongs with the prepositions of path and is included below only so the two are not confused.
entries.see also: in the way of, in the capacity of, as, in terms of

entries.meaning: Declares that what follows is true inside one stated set of rules and nowhere else. It is how American drafters make a word mean something locally without disturbing its ordinary meaning.
examples: For purposes of this section, "resident" means anyone domiciled in the state.
The two subsidiaries are treated as one employer for purposes of the statute.
She is not a public figure for purposes of the defamation analysis.
Stock options are counted as wages for purposes of the overtime calculation.
For purposes of the audit, the fiscal year ends September 30.
For purposes of calculating seniority, unpaid leave does not count.

senses.head: Restricting a definition to a named text
examples: For purposes of this section, "resident" means anyone domiciled in the state.
The two subsidiaries are treated as one employer for purposes of the statute.
She is not a public figure for purposes of the defamation analysis.

senses.head: Restricting a computation or a test to one procedure
examples: Stock options are counted as wages for purposes of the overtime calculation.
For purposes of the audit, the fiscal year ends September 30.
For purposes of calculating seniority, unpaid leave does not count.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /fɚ ˈpɜrpəsəz ə/ (for reduces to /fɚ/, also written /fər/, and final of to /ə/) — fur-PUR-puh-siz-uv
entries.русский: юр. для целей — ограничивает определение или расчёт рамками названного текста
entries.register: formal and legal — the standard American drafting phrase for fencing off a definition
entries.complement: a noun phrase, most often naming a statute, section, rule, article, or analysis (for purposes of this Article, for purposes of the overtime calculation); a gerund is possible and common in tax drafting (for purposes of calculating basis); never a clause of any kind.
entries.pattern: For purposes of [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] for purposes of [noun phrase]
entries.variants: for the purposes of (with the article — the British and Commonwealth drafting form, and still seen in older American statutes); solely for purposes of (the emphatic drafting version)
entries.contrast: The article and the number decide which phrase you have, and they are not interchangeable. For the purpose of + gerund states an aim and belongs with the prepositions of purpose — for the purpose of raising money — while for purposes of + a named text restricts a definition to one domain: for purposes of this section, "employee" includes a contractor. Writing for the purpose of this section is the usual slip, and it says something the drafter did not mean. Against in the case of, which subdivides a class of people or things, this phrase fences off a body of rules; against as a matter of, it limits where a definition applies rather than what kind of consideration is in play. See for the purpose of for the purpose sense.
entries.see also: in the case of, as a matter of, in point of, with respect to, for the purpose of

entries.meaning: Picks one member out of a class and states how the general rule applies to it. The phrase earns its place when a real class is genuinely being subdivided, and it is padding the rest of the time.
examples: In the case of part-time employees, the waiting period is ninety days.
The deduction is capped at two thousand dollars, except in the case of farm equipment.
In the case of the Denver office, the lease runs another four years.
In the case of a tie, the chair votes.
Refunds are issued automatically, though not in the case of tickets bought through a reseller.
In the case of who inherits the house, the will is silent.
entries.русский: в случае с, что касается — выделяет одного из класса и говорит, как к нему применимо правило
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (in the case of subletting without notice), or a fused wh-nominal (in the case of who inherits); never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: In the case of [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] in the case of [noun phrase] · except in the case of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The article changes the meaning completely, and this is the error to watch. In case of — no the — is contingency, an if: in case of fire, use the stairs, treated with in case of. In the case of singles out one member of a class already under discussion and says how the general rule lands on it: in the case of the Denver office, the lease runs another four years. Swapping them produces nonsense in both directions. Against as for, which switches topic conversationally and often with a sting, in the case of is analytic and neutral. Against as far as X is concerned, it subdivides a class rather than restricting a claim to a domain. Editors cut it whenever the sentence survives without it: in the case of older buildings, permits take longer is just older buildings take longer to permit.
entries.see also: as for, as far as X is concerned, in the matter of, in case of, with respect to

entries.meaning: Restricts a claim to how one party sees it, with the standing implication that somebody else sees it differently. It is the ordinary American way of saying that a legal, professional, or social fiction is in force.
examples: In the eyes of the law, the two companies are a single employer.
The apology cost him nothing and gained him nothing in the eyes of the staff.
In the eyes of her students, the whole semester was a disaster.
A signed receipt is enough in the eyes of the auditors.
The sale made him, in the eyes of the neighborhood, the man who lost the park.
In the eyes of the IRS, a hobby that turns a profit three years out of five is a business.
entries.pronunciation note: in-thee-EYEZ-uv · note the article: the is /ði/ here rather than /ðə/, because eyes begins with a vowel
entries.русский: в глазах — с точки зрения одной стороны: in the eyes of the law «в глазах закона»
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a person, a group, or an institution capable of holding a view — the law, the court, his colleagues, the public, God. No gerund and no clause of any kind (✗ in the eyes of paying late, ✗ in the eyes of that he lied). A pronoun object is stilted; American English switches to the possessive frame in my eyes, in her eyes, and ✗ in the eyes of me is not English.
entries.pattern: In the eyes of [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] in the eyes of [noun phrase] · possessive: in [possessive] eyes
entries.contrast: Against in the opinion of, which reports a judgment somebody actually formed and usually stated, this phrase reports how a thing is perceived, whether or not anyone has said so — which is exactly why in the eyes of the law is idiomatic while ✗ in the opinion of the law is not: the law has a standing view, not an opinion it arrived at last Tuesday. Against in the sight of, its archaic religious twin, this is the living modern phrase and has taken over every secular job. The plural is fixed: ✗ in the eye of the law, and the eye of the storm is a different metaphor altogether.
entries.see also: in the opinion of, in the sight of, on the face of, as far as X is concerned, according to

entries.meaning: Attributes a judgment to the person or body that formed it, and in doing so concedes that the judgment is a judgment and could be wrong. In an opinion letter that concession is the entire point of the phrase.
examples: In the opinion of the court, the statute is unconstitutional as applied.
The shares are freely tradable in the opinion of counsel.
In the opinion of the examining physician, she can return to light duty in six weeks.
The statements present fairly, in the opinion of the auditors, the company's financial position.
In the opinion of two of the three engineers, the bracket had already failed.
Nothing in the record supports the finding, in the opinion of the dissent.
entries.pronunciation note: in-thee-uh-PIN-yun-uv · the is /ði/ before the vowel of opinion, and the stress sits on -pin-
entries.русский: по мнению — офиц.: приписывает суждение тому, кто его вынес, признавая его суждением
entries.register: formal; standard in judicial opinions, opinion letters, audit reports, and medical evaluations
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a person or a deliberating body — the court, counsel, the examining physician, the committee. No gerund and no clause of any kind (✗ in the opinion of that the claim fails). With a first- or second-person referent English switches to the possessive: in my opinion, in our opinion, and ✗ in the opinion of me is impossible.
entries.pattern: In the opinion of [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] in the opinion of [noun phrase] · possessive: in [possessive] opinion
entries.variants: in the view of (interchangeable and a shade less formal); in the judgment of (implies a decision reached rather than a belief held); in my opinion, and its internet clipping IMO, for the first person
entries.contrast: Against according to, which reports what somebody said, this phrase attributes a judgment — and it is the standard hedge by which a professional signs a conclusion without guaranteeing it: in the opinion of counsel, the shares are exempt quietly concedes that a court could disagree. Against in the eyes of, which is perception and needs no deliberation, this is deliberation and needs a deliberator. The noun stays singular: ✗ in the opinions of the court.
entries.see also: in the eyes of, in the words of, as far as X is concerned, according to, pace

entries.meaning: The biblical and liturgical phrase for divine judgment. An American hears it at weddings and funerals and in scripture, and encounters it in writing that is reaching consciously for the seventeenth century.
examples: We are gathered here in the sight of God to join these two in marriage.
The psalm asks that the words of his mouth be acceptable in the sight of the Lord.
All are equal in the sight of heaven, whatever the parish register says.
He believed the debt was forgiven in the sight of God and unforgiven everywhere else.
The pamphlet argued that the trade was an abomination in the sight of the Almighty.
In the sight of the moral law, she wrote, intention counts for everything.
entries.pronunciation note: in-thuh-SYTE-uv · unlike in the eyes of, the article stays /ðə/ here, because sight begins with a consonant
entries.русский: устар./церк. пред лицом, в очах — библейское: in the sight of God «пред Богом»
entries.register: archaic and religious — Early Modern English, fixed in the language by the King James Bible of 1611 and kept alive by liturgy; in modern prose it is a quotation, a liturgical formula, or a deliberate period effect, and never ordinary usage
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming God, a deity, or — in older moral and legal English — heaven, men, the law. No gerund and no clause of any kind. Extending it past that narrow set reads as parody: ✗ in the sight of the zoning board.
entries.pattern: In the sight of [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] in the sight of [noun phrase] · fixed: in the sight of God
entries.variants: in God's sight (the possessive form, equally biblical); before God (the plain modern equivalent); in the eyes of (the living replacement in every secular use)
entries.contrast: Do not reach for this as an ordinary modern preposition. In the eyes of has taken over all of its secular work: in the eyes of the law is current American English, while in the sight of the law is dated to the point of costume. Distinguish it also from the spatial within sight of (they anchored within sight of the shore), which is about literal visibility and belongs with the prepositions of place; in the sight of is never spatial in modern use, however plainly the metaphor started there.
entries.see also: in the eyes of, in the opinion of, in the words of, touching, anent

entries.meaning: Restricts a statement to a single dimension. In modern American English it survives almost entirely in in point of fact and, in legal writing, in point of law.
examples: In point of fact, the building was condemned two years earlier.
He was, in point of fact, never employed there at all.
The claim is unreviewable in point of law.
In point of law the two instruments are identical, whatever the parties intended.
In point of time, the second signature came first.
The two editions are identical in point of substance, if not of price.

senses.head: In point of fact — a stuffier, more insistent actually, and nearly always corrective
examples: In point of fact, the building was condemned two years earlier.
He was, in point of fact, never employed there at all.

senses.head: In point of law — restricting a claim to the legal dimension
body: Compare as a matter of law, which is the commoner American phrasing.
examples: The claim is unreviewable in point of law.
In point of law the two instruments are identical, whatever the parties intended.

senses.head: Any other single dimension — archaic outside the two fixed phrases
examples: In point of time, the second signature came first.
The two editions are identical in point of substance, if not of price.

entries.русский: книжн. в отношении — живёт в in point of fact «на самом деле» и in point of law «юридически»
entries.register: formal, verging on archaic outside two fixed phrases
entries.complement: a bare abstract noun — fact, law, time, form, accuracy — with no article. No gerund, no clause, no ordinary concrete noun.
entries.pattern: In point of [bare abstract noun], [clause] · [clause] in point of [bare abstract noun]
entries.contrast: Do not confuse it with a case in point (an illustrating example), to the point (relevant), or up to a point (partially) — same noun, unrelated idioms. In point of fact is a stuffier, more insistent actually, and like actually it is usually corrective: it announces that what follows contradicts what was just assumed.
entries.see also: in terms of, as a matter of, in the matter of, on the score of, with respect to

examples: Measured in terms of calories, the two meals are nearly identical.
He explained the whole conflict in terms of water rights.
The contract is priced in terms of barrels, not dollars.
In terms of the timeline, we're about two weeks behind.
She's strongest in terms of client work.
In terms of what it costs, nobody has given us a number.
In terms of the weather, Saturday looks better.

senses.head: Using the concepts, units, or framework of something stated
body: Precise and defensible.
examples: Measured in terms of calories, the two meals are nearly identical.
He explained the whole conflict in terms of water rights.
The contract is priced in terms of barrels, not dollars.

senses.head: As regards, with respect to
body: Extremely common in speech and almost always removable.
examples: In terms of the timeline, we're about two weeks behind.
She's strongest in terms of client work.
In terms of what it costs, nobody has given us a number.
In terms of the weather, Saturday looks better.

entries.русский: в понятиях, в пересчёте на — точный смысл; в разг. «что касается» — лишние слова
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a fused wh-nominal (in terms of what it costs); never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in terms of [noun phrase] · In terms of [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: The plural is fixed — in term of is an error. More importantly, two very different uses share the phrase, and only one survives editing. Sense 1 states the units or framework of a measurement and is precise. Sense 2 is a filler about, and it is the single most frequently cut phrase in American editing: in terms of the budget, we're fine is just the budget is fine.
entries.see also: with respect to, as far as X is concerned, in relation to, as regards

examples: Do you have anything in the way of vegetarian options?
The apartment offers very little in the way of storage.
He'd received nothing in the way of an explanation.
There isn't much in the way of competition in that market.
A parked truck stood in the way of the ambulance.
Nothing now stands in the way of the sale.

senses.head: In the category of, as regards — after a word of quantity
examples: Do you have anything in the way of vegetarian options?
The apartment offers very little in the way of storage.
He'd received nothing in the way of an explanation.
There isn't much in the way of competition in that market.

senses.head: Literally blocking — a different construction, listed for contrast
examples: A parked truck stood in the way of the ambulance.
Nothing now stands in the way of the sale.

entries.русский: в смысле, по части — после слов количества: little in the way of proof «доказательств негусто»
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund; never a clause of any kind. In sense 1 a quantity word (anything, much, little, nothing) almost always comes first.
entries.pattern: [quantity word: anything, much, little, nothing] in the way of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The topic sense almost always follows a quantifier, and usually a negative or a question — anything in the way of, little in the way of, nothing in the way of. Strip the quantifier and you get the literal blocking sense (standing in the way of the merger), which is a wholly different construction and the reason this idiom is slowly disappearing. By way of covers nearly the same ground in sense 3 and sounds less antique.
entries.see also: by way of, as far as X is concerned, as regards, in terms of

entries.meaning: Restricts a claim to what the surface of a thing shows. In conversation that restriction is a hedge and something is about to be taken back; in a courtroom it is a rule about how far outside the document a judge may look.
examples: On the face of it, the offer is generous.
On the face of it nothing had changed, but every one of the staff had been reassigned.
The complaint fails on the face of the pleadings.
On the face of the statute, the exemption reaches only nonprofits.
The deed is void on its face.
It is the finest hardware store on the face of the earth.
There is no reason on the face of the earth to drive that far for gas.

senses.head: On the face of it — judging by appearances, and usually the setup for a contradiction
body: The commonest use in ordinary American English, and it almost never stands alone.
examples: On the face of it, the offer is generous.
On the face of it nothing had changed, but every one of the staff had been reassigned.

senses.head: Legal: from the document itself, without looking outside it
body: Here the phrase is a rule about evidence, and the possessive form on its face is commoner still.
examples: The complaint fails on the face of the pleadings.
On the face of the statute, the exemption reaches only nonprofits.
The deed is void on its face.

senses.head: Not a limiter at all — the fixed intensifier "on the face of the earth."
body: It names a place and concedes nothing.
examples: It is the finest hardware store on the face of the earth.
There is no reason on the face of the earth to drive that far for gas.

entries.pronunciation note: ahn-thuh-FACE-uv · in the fixed phrase on the face of it the final of it runs together as /əvɪt/ or simply /əvɪ/
entries.русский: на первый взгляд — on the face of it, обычно перед возражением; юр. «из самого документа»
entries.register: neutral in on the face of it; legal in on the face of the record
entries.complement: a noun phrase — most often the pronoun it, otherwise a document, record, or instrument (the complaint, the statute, the deed). No gerund and no clause of any kind (✗ on the face of that the numbers do not add up). The possessive frame on its face, on their face is the commoner American legal form and takes no object at all.
entries.pattern: On the face of it, [clause] · [clause] on the face of [document] · possessive: [noun phrase] on its face
entries.variants: on its face, on their face (the standard American legal forms); at first blush (the conversational equivalent); facially, the adverb, as in facially invalid; the Latin prima facie, which is in formal, Latin, and archaic prepositions
entries.contrast: Two senses, and they differ in what they concede. On the face of it nearly always sets up a but: it grants the appearance in order to deny the substance. The legal sense grants nothing — invalid on the face of the statute means the defect is visible without going outside the document, which is a rule about what evidence a court may look at, not a hedge about appearances. Against in the eyes of, which fences a claim to one party's perception, this fences it to what the surface of a thing shows. And keep it apart from the fixed intensifier on the face of the earth, which names a place rather than an appearance.
entries.see also: in the eyes of, in point of, as a matter of, within the meaning of, as far as X is concerned

entries.meaning: Narrows the discussion to one domain, usually to say the general rule does not hold there. It is the workhorse of American conversational framing.
examples: When it comes to pricing, nobody in the region touches them.
The state is generous when it comes to unemployment benefits.
When it comes to who actually decides, the org chart tells you nothing.
She's fearless in a meeting. When it comes to small talk, she's hopeless.
He'll argue about anything. When it comes to apologizing, he goes quiet.
When it comes to raising money, he'd rather do anything else.
When it came to signing the lease, both of them found reasons to wait.

senses.head: Restricting a claim to one domain
examples: When it comes to pricing, nobody in the region touches them.
The state is generous when it comes to unemployment benefits.
When it comes to who actually decides, the org chart tells you nothing.

senses.head: Setting up a contrast with what was just said
examples: She's fearless in a meeting. When it comes to small talk, she's hopeless.
He'll argue about anything. When it comes to apologizing, he goes quiet.

senses.head: With a gerund, where the domain is an activity
examples: When it comes to raising money, he'd rather do anything else.
When it came to signing the lease, both of them found reasons to wait.

entries.pronunciation note: wen-it-KUMZ-too · the stress sits on comes; when and the final to both reduce, and in fast speech the whole frame runs together as /wənɪtˈkʌmztə/
entries.русский: когда речь заходит о, что касается — разг.; несмотря на when, времени не обозначает
entries.register: neutral to informal; extremely common in American speech, journalism, and advertising
entries.type: complex and fossilized from a clause — a when-clause that has hardened into a topic-marking preposition, and no longer names a time
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun (when it comes to me, never when it comes to I), gerund (when it comes to raising money), or a fused wh-nominal (when it comes to who actually decides); ✗ never a finite that-clause (✗ when it comes to that the rent is late). The to is a preposition, not the infinitive marker, which is exactly why a verb after it takes -ing: ✗ when it comes to raise money → when it comes to raising money.
entries.pattern: When it comes to [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] when it comes to [noun phrase] · past: when it came to [noun phrase]
entries.variants: when it came to (past, and the only inflection the frame allows); when it comes down to (adds "in the end, after everything else is stripped away"); if it comes to (hypothetical, and often a threat)
entries.cross-class test: the frame is a preposition only when a noun phrase follows to and no clause follows the frame's own verb; ordinary temporal when it comes to a vote we'll know — where a vote is an event on the clock — is the literal when-clause it grew out of.
entries.contrast: The living American equivalent of as far as X is concerned, and much the commoner of the two in speech. It differs from as for in that it does not switch topics — it narrows to a domain inside the topic already running, and it very often sets up a contrast with what was just said: He's careless with money. When it comes to his tools, he's meticulous. Editors treat it as padding in formal prose exactly the way they treat in terms of, and the cure is the same: make the object the subject of the sentence.
entries.see also: as far as X is concerned, as for, in terms of, on the subject of, with respect to

entries.meaning: The legal test phrase. It takes an ordinary English word that some statute has redefined and asks whether this particular thing counts as one, and the answer is binding nowhere else.
examples: The company is an affiliate within the meaning of Rule 144.
Drivers who set their own hours may not be employees within the meaning of the Act.
The letter is not a security within the meaning of Section 2(a)(1).
The board found an unfair labor practice within the meaning of Section 8(a)(1).
A stepchild is a child within the meaning of the policy.
Nothing the county did amounts to a taking within the meaning of the Fifth Amendment.
entries.pronunciation note: with-IN-thuh-MEE-ning-uv · also /wɪθˈɪn/ with a voiceless th; the phrase carries two stresses, on -in and on mean-, and only the little words between and after them reduce
entries.русский: юр. в значении, придаваемом — подпадает ли предмет под определение данного закона
entries.register: legal — the standard American phrase for asking whether a thing falls inside a written definition
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a text or a defined term: a statute, a section, a rule, a policy, a clause (within the meaning of Section 3(a)(1), within the meaning of the Act). No gerund and no clause of any kind (✗ within the meaning of that he was employed).
entries.pattern: [X] is or is not [a defined term] within the meaning of [text] · [noun phrase] within the meaning of [text]
entries.contrast: The third member of the drafting trio, and the one that does the arguing. As used in writes a definition, as defined in points at one, and within the meaning of claims that something falls inside one — which is why this is the phrase that turns up in the sentence a court actually has to decide. Against for purposes of, which fences a rule to a body of law, this fences a classification to a body of law: she is not an employee within the meaning of the Act leaves entirely open that she is an employee for every other purpose in the world. Where an American meets it: an SEC filing, an NLRB or EEOC decision, an immigration notice, a tax opinion, and the denial letter from an insurer.
entries.see also: as defined in, as used in, for purposes of, in the case of, as a matter of

entries.meaning: The role preposition, and one of the highest-frequency words in English. Senses 1 through 5 are all prepositional; sense 6 is included because the same spelling covers a conjunction that learners constantly confuse with it.
examples: She spent eleven years as a public defender.
As treasurer, he signs every check over five thousand dollars.
He was hired as a consultant and stayed as head of the department.
We used a milk crate as a nightstand for most of that year.
The gym doubles as a storm shelter.
He came to the party as a bag of jelly beans.
She was cast as Lady Macbeth three seasons running.
As a child, she spent every summer on the lake.
As a young attorney he took whatever walked through the door.
The letter was dismissed as a hoax within a day.
Most economists regard the figure as unreliable.
He's known as the only person who can fix that machine.
Skipping the deposition would count as defaulting.
The lights went out as she reached the landing.
As the roads were closed, we stayed another night.

senses.head: The job, office, or role a person holds
examples: She spent eleven years as a public defender.
As treasurer, he signs every check over five thousand dollars.
He was hired as a consultant and stayed as head of the department.

senses.head: The function a thing is put to
examples: We used a milk crate as a nightstand for most of that year.
The gym doubles as a storm shelter.

senses.head: In the character of — costume, casting, or disguise
examples: He came to the party as a bag of jelly beans.
She was cast as Lady Macbeth three seasons running.

senses.head: At a stage of life, or in a stated condition
body: Here the noun phrase names not an office but a period or a state.
examples: As a child, she spent every summer on the lake.
As a young attorney he took whatever walked through the door.

senses.head: The status a verb of classification assigns
body: After regard, see, describe, treat, define, count, cite, dismiss, know — and note that this is the one sense that admits an adjective or a participle in place of a noun.
examples: The letter was dismissed as a hoax within a day.
Most economists regard the figure as unreliable.
He's known as the only person who can fix that machine.
Skipping the deposition would count as defaulting.

senses.head: Not a preposition — the conjunction of time and cause, which takes a whole clause and governs no object
examples: The lights went out as she reached the landing.
As the roads were closed, we stayed another night.

entries.русский: в качестве, как — роль или назначение; в русском часто творительный: work as a nurse — медсестрой
entries.type: simple — the same word is also a subordinating conjunction of time and cause (as I was leaving), half of the comparative correlative as … as, and a relative pronoun after such and the same (such delays as we saw)
entries.complement: a noun phrase, bare (as chair, as treasurer) or with an article (as a nurse), with any pronoun in the objective case (cast as me, never ✗ as I). After verbs of classification it also takes an adjective phrase (regard the figure as unreliable, dismissed the claim as premature) and a participial phrase (described as having failed to file, counts as cheating). Never a finite clause — a clause after as means you have the conjunction, not the preposition — and never a bare gerund in the role sense: ✗ He works as driving a bus → He works as a bus driver.
entries.pattern: [verb] as [noun phrase] · As [noun phrase], [clause] · [verb] [object] as [noun phrase or adjective phrase], with verbs of classification: regard/see/describe/treat/define/cite/use/dismiss X as Y
entries.contrast: As versus like is the central rule. As your doctor, I'd advise against it means the speaker is the doctor; Like your doctor, I'd advise against it means the speaker is somebody else who happens to agree. In careful American English, as takes a role and like takes a resemblance. Two corollaries: such as introduces genuine members of a set (fruit such as pears) and informal like does the same job in speech; and like used as a conjunction (like I said, like I told you) is thoroughly established in American speech but still cut in edited prose, where the conjunction is as. Against for: mistaken for a doctor means misidentified, taken as a compliment means interpreted. Cross-class test — the object: She works as a nurse is the preposition (object a nurse, a noun phrase) against She works as I do (conjunction, whole clause); as tall as I am is the comparative correlative; and in such delays as we saw, as is a relative pronoun. Anything headed by as that is completed by a clause is the conjunction, and that includes the compounds as if, as though, as soon as, as long as, and as far as — none of them takes an object, and none of them may be stranded.
entries.see also: qua, in the capacity of, in the role of, in the guise of, for

entries.meaning: Separates the hat from the person wearing it. It matters where someone holds more than one office and only one of them is acting.
examples: She signed in the capacity of executor, not in her personal capacity.
He attended in the capacity of an observer and asked no questions.
Statements made in his capacity as spokesman are attributable to the agency.
The auditor may not serve in the capacity of a director.
In her capacity as department chair, she controls the teaching schedule.
Any liability incurred in the capacity of agent falls on the principal.
entries.русский: офиц. в качестве, в должности — когда у человека несколько ролей и действует одна
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a role, generally without an article; never a clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: in the capacity of [role] · in [possessive] capacity as [role] · acting in the capacity of [role]
entries.variants: in one's capacity as (in her capacity as trustee) — much the commoner American form; acting in the capacity of
entries.contrast: The two frames take different prepositions and mixing them is the usual error: the article-less version takes of (in the capacity of trustee), the possessive version takes as (in her capacity as trustee). In the capacity as is wrong. Against plain as, this phrase exists to insist that only one of a person's several roles is in play — which is precisely why lawyers use it.
entries.see also: as, qua, in the role of, in the person of

entries.meaning: Names the shape an abstraction turned out to have. The sentence introduces something general — help, pressure, evidence, a warning, compensation — and this phrase says what it concretely was.
examples: Relief arrived in the form of a federal grant.
The company offered compensation in the form of store credit.
Pressure came in the form of three letters from the state attorney general.
The only evidence is circumstantial, in the form of a parking receipt.
He got his answer in the form of a locked door.
Support was offered in the form of forgiving the first two months' rent.
entries.русский: в виде, в форме — конкретное воплощение отвлечённого: help in the form of a loan
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (help in the form of forgiving two months' rent); never a clause of any kind.
entries.pattern: [abstract noun] in the form of [noun phrase] · [clause] in the form of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The neutral member of the guise family and the one American writers actually need. In the guise of asserts that the appearance is a false front; in the form of only states the shape the thing turned out to have and passes no judgment — compare a tax increase in the guise of a user fee (an accusation) with relief in the form of a rent credit (a description). Against in the person of, which is reserved for human beings, in the form of covers things, and applying it to a person is faintly comic unless the comedy is intended. Against by way of sense 1, which names a purpose (flowers by way of apology), this phrase names a substance.
entries.see also: in the guise of, in the person of, as, by way of, in the role of

entries.meaning: Assigns a role and disbelieves it in the same breath.
examples: The god appears in the guise of an old woman at the crossroads.
He turned up at the border in the guise of a relief worker.
The bill arrived in the guise of a routine reauthorization.
It's censorship in the guise of quality control.
They cut the program in the guise of streamlining.
The surveillance ran for years under the guise of routine maintenance.
She got into the building under the guise of delivering flowers.
The fee was raised under the guise of covering administrative costs.

senses.head: Wearing an assumed shape or identity — the literary and mythological use
examples: The god appears in the guise of an old woman at the crossroads.
He turned up at the border in the guise of a relief worker.

senses.head: Presented as something more innocuous than it is — the accusation
examples: The bill arrived in the guise of a routine reauthorization.
It's censorship in the guise of quality control.
They cut the program in the guise of streamlining.

senses.head: Under the guise of — the commoner American form, and the more openly accusatory
body: It takes a gerund far more readily than in the guise of does.
examples: The surveillance ran for years under the guise of routine maintenance.
She got into the building under the guise of delivering flowers.
The fee was raised under the guise of covering administrative costs.

entries.русский: книжн. под видом, в обличье — чужой облик; чаще амер. under the guise of «под предлогом»
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (under the guise of protecting consumers); never a clause of any kind.
entries.pattern: [clause] in the guise of [noun phrase] · In the guise of [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.variants: under the guise of — the commoner form in American English by a wide margin and the more accusatory of the two; in the guise of keeps a faint literary and mythological flavor (the god in the guise of a swan), while under the guise of belongs to investigative journalism and litigation. Under the pretext of and under cover of are the plainer synonyms.
entries.contrast: In the form of is neutral and merely describes a shape; in the guise of is skeptical and asserts that the appearance is false. Against as, which takes the role at face value, this phrase always implies a disguise or a pretext — so a tax increase in the guise of a user fee is an accusation, not a description, and a writer who does not intend the accusation should use in the form of.
entries.see also: in the form of, as, in the role of, in the person of, by way of

entries.meaning: Classifies something loosely, as near enough to a named kind to be described that way. In ordinary prose the looseness is the point; in tax and pleading the same phrase becomes a hard test of what a thing really is.
examples: He offered something in the nature of an apology and then changed the subject.
What she gave us was nothing in the nature of a straight answer.
There is a room in the nature of a conservatory at the back of the house.
A payment in the nature of interest is taxable as interest.
The plaintiff sought relief in the nature of mandamus.
Charges in the nature of penalties are not deductible.
It is in the nature of committees to postpone the hard question.
Some loss of pressure is in the nature of the system and cannot be engineered out.

senses.head: Roughly, something like — the hedged classification
body: Almost always after something, anything, or nothing.
examples: He offered something in the nature of an apology and then changed the subject.
What she gave us was nothing in the nature of a straight answer.
There is a room in the nature of a conservatory at the back of the house.

senses.head: Legal and tax: characterized as, whatever the label on it says
body: Here the phrase is a test, not a hedge.
examples: A payment in the nature of interest is taxable as interest.
The plaintiff sought relief in the nature of mandamus.
Charges in the nature of penalties are not deductible.

senses.head: Not a topic marker — the predicate frame in which nature means innate character
body: Nothing is being classified, and the phrase governs no topic.
examples: It is in the nature of committees to postpone the hard question.
Some loss of pressure is in the nature of the system and cannot be engineered out.

entries.pronunciation note: in-thuh-NAY-chur-uv · the stress is on na-, and the -ture is /tʃɚ/, never /tjʊr/
entries.русский: вроде, наподобие — смягчённая классификация; юр. «по своему характеру, по существу»
entries.register: formal in ordinary prose; a term of art in tax, pleading, and accounting
entries.complement: a noun phrase, characteristically with the indefinite article (in the nature of an apology), and in the legal use a bare abstract noun (in the nature of interest, in the nature of mandamus). A gerund is grammatical but stiff (in the nature of settling old scores), and no clause of any kind is possible (✗ in the nature of that he apologized).
entries.pattern: [something / anything / nothing] in the nature of [noun phrase] · [noun phrase] in the nature of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Against in the form of, which names the concrete shape a thing turned out to have and commits to it, in the nature of hedges: relief in the form of a rent credit was a rent credit, while something in the nature of a rent credit was merely close enough to one to describe that way. Against in the guise of, it makes no accusation — it classifies rather than unmasks. In legal and tax writing the hedge hardens into a test: a payment in the nature of interest is taxed as interest whatever the parties chose to call it, and that substance-over-form move is the whole reason the phrase survives. Keep it clear of the unrelated predicate construction in which nature means innate character.
entries.see also: in the form of, in the guise of, as, in the way of, by way of

entries.meaning: Identifies the human being in whom an abstraction shows up.
examples: Relief arrived in the person of a retired paramedic who lived two doors down.
The opposition found a leader in the person of a thirty-year-old schoolteacher.
The company's institutional memory survives in the person of one payroll clerk.
Authority was present in the person of the deputy commissioner.
He met his match in the person of his own daughter.
entries.русский: книжн. в лице — называет человека, в котором воплотилось отвлечённое понятие
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a person, usually a name or a title; never a clause.
entries.pattern: [abstract noun or clause] in the person of [name]
entries.contrast: In the form of does the same job for things (help arrived in the form of a tow truck); in the person of is reserved for human beings and is faintly grand. It names the individual who embodies something abstract that the sentence has just introduced — the structure is always "X arrived, and X turned out to be this specific person."
entries.see also: in the capacity of, in the role of, as, in the guise of

entries.meaning: Names the part somebody is playing, on a stage or off one.
examples: In the role of Willy Loman, an understudy nobody had heard of.
She found herself in the role of referee between two departments.
He was miscast in the role of the reasonable one.
The agency acts in the role of clearinghouse for the whole region.
In the role of narrator, the older brother is not to be trusted.
entries.русский: в роли — называет исполняемую роль, на сцене и вне её
entries.complement: a noun phrase, usually with an article or a proper name; never a clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in the role of [noun phrase] · In the role of [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: Theatrical by default — in a cast list it is the standard formula — and extended from there to any adopted function. Outside casting, plain as is shorter and nearly always better: she acted as mediator beats she acted in the role of mediator. Against in the capacity of, this phrase is descriptive where that one is jurisdictional.
entries.see also: as, in the capacity of, in the guise of, in the person of

entries.meaning: The philosopher's preposition. It splits a thing from itself so that only one of its roles is on the table.
examples: The university qua employer has obligations it does not have qua educator.
He is studying the novel qua commodity, not qua art.
The state qua state cannot hold a religious belief.
What interests her is the building qua structure, not qua landmark.
A judge qua judge has no opinions, which is a useful fiction.
entries.pronunciation note: KWAY (also KWAH) · no weak form — it is always stressed, being the pivot of the construction it appears in
entries.русский: книжн./филос. как таковой, в качестве — лат.: вещь берётся лишь в одной её ипостаси
entries.register: formal and academic — philosophy, law, and theory
entries.type: simple (Latin, ablative feminine of quī "who, which")
entries.complement: a bare noun phrase, characteristically without an article and very often repeating the noun it follows (the state qua state). Never a clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [noun] qua [noun] · [clause] qua [noun]
entries.contrast: Qua means "in the capacity of, considered strictly as, in that thing's character of" and its job is to isolate one aspect of a thing from its other aspects. As would serve most readers just as well; qua signals a technical register and a deliberate act of analytical separation. Note the pronunciation: /kweɪ/ is the established English form and the spelling-based /kwɑ/ is also heard, but it is never /kwɔ/, and qua is not related to the qua- of quality or the quo of status quo.
entries.see also: as, in the capacity of, in terms of, in the role of

entries.meaning: Names the official authority that made a wrongful act possible. It is the hinge on which American civil-rights liability turns, which is why it is worth knowing that it describes a source of power rather than a lawful exercise of it.
examples: The suit alleges that the deputies acted under color of state law.
Section 1983 reaches only conduct under color of law.
A private security guard is not ordinarily acting under color of state authority.
He collected the fees under color of office and kept them.
The indictment charges deprivation of rights under color of law.
Evictions carried out under color of a forged court order are void.

senses.head: The statutory test — conduct made possible by public office
examples: The suit alleges that the deputies acted under color of state law.
Section 1983 reaches only conduct under color of law.
A private security guard is not ordinarily acting under color of state authority.

senses.head: Abuse of a particular office, outside the § 1983 formula
examples: He collected the fees under color of office and kept them.
The indictment charges deprivation of rights under color of law.
Evictions carried out under color of a forged court order are void.

entries.русский: юр. под видом законного, с использованием служебного положения — under color of law
entries.register: legal — a term of art in American civil-rights and criminal practice, and rare outside it
entries.complement: a bare noun phrase naming an authority, office, or body of law, with no article: color of law, color of state law, color of office, color of authority. A gerund is not idiomatic, and no clause of any kind is possible.
entries.pattern: [verb] under color of [bare noun phrase] · acting under color of [bare noun phrase]
entries.variants: under color of law — the fixed statutory phrase of 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and 18 U.S.C. § 242, and the form nearly every occurrence takes; under color of office; under color of authority; the related adjective colorable (a colorable claim), which means "plausible enough to argue," not "false"
entries.contrast: The legal sibling of under the guise of. Both say a role is being used as cover, but they are not interchangeable: under the guise of is a journalist's accusation of pretext, while under color of is a jurisdictional test — an officer acts under color of law whenever the act was made possible by the office, authorized or not, which is precisely why the phrase does not mean "lawfully." Against plain as and in the capacity of, which take the office at face value, this phrase says the office was the instrument. Note the vocabulary trap: color here is the old legal sense "appearance, semblance, pretense," unrelated to the everyday noun — and the American spelling has no u, in this phrase as everywhere else.
entries.see also: in the guise of, in the capacity of, as, in the role of, by virtue of

entries.meaning: Hands the sentence over to somebody else's phrasing and takes responsibility for the words being theirs. It is the workhorse of quotation in American journalism and judicial writing alike.
examples: In the words of one investigator, the file had been "cleaned within an inch of its life."
The program was, in the words of its own director, an experiment nobody expected to survive.
In the words of the statute, the notice must be "actual and timely."
He described the layoffs, in the words of the memo, as a realignment.
In the words of the dissent, the majority has quietly rewritten the clause.
She wanted to hear it, in the words of her grandmother, from the horse's mouth.
entries.русский: по словам, говоря словами — вводит чужую формулировку и приписывает её автору
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a speaker or a text — a person, a court, a statute, a report, a witness. No gerund and no clause of any kind (✗ in the words of that he resigned). For pronouns English switches to the possessive: in his own words, in her words, and ✗ in the words of me is not English.
entries.pattern: In the words of [source], "[quotation]" · [clause], in the words of [source], [quoted phrase] · possessive: in [possessive] own words
entries.variants: in the words of the statute and in the words of the court (the legal uses); in his own words (insisting the phrasing is unaltered); to quote [source] (the plain equivalent); in a word and in other words, which are not this phrase at all — they take no object and simply reframe what the writer has already said
entries.contrast: Against according to, which reports the substance of what somebody said, in the words of vouches for the phrasing — so what follows should be the source's actual words or something very close to them, and putting your own summary after it is a small dishonesty that readers notice. Against in the opinion of, which attributes a judgment, this attributes only the wording. Cross-class test — the object: in the words of the report is the preposition and has an object; in other words and in a word govern nothing and are discourse adverbials.
entries.see also: in the opinion of, in the eyes of, pace, as per, according to

entries.meaning: Concedes, politely and in passing, that a named authority disagrees with what you are about to say.
examples: Pace Freud, the dream literature has moved on considerably.
The manuscript is, pace Robertson, almost certainly a later copy.
Pace my colleagues in the department, the reform did work.
Attendance has risen every year (pace the recent editorials).
Pace Aristotle, not every polity aims at the good.
entries.pronunciation note: PAY-see (also PAH-chay) · no weak form — it is a two-syllable Latin word carrying its own stress, and it never reduces to the /peɪs/ of the English noun
entries.русский: книжн. при всём уважении к — лат.: оговорка, что названный авторитет думает иначе
entries.complement: a personal name, or a noun phrase naming a person or an authority. Never a clause, never a gerund, never an abstract topic.
entries.pattern: Pace [name], [clause] · [clause] (pace [name])
entries.contrast: A homograph, not a sense, of the everyday noun and verb pace /peɪs/ meaning "step" — different word, different origin, different pronunciation. And it is emphatically not a synonym for according to; it means close to the opposite: "with apologies to X, who argues otherwise." Writers who use it as according to invert their own sentence.
entries.see also: qua, vis-à-vis, apropos of, notwithstanding

entries.meaning: The conversational hinge. It licenses a change of subject by pretending the change was inevitable.
examples: Speaking of the weather, did you ever get the gutters cleaned?
Speaking of which, your brother called twice.
Speaking of people who never answer email — has anyone heard from Dana?
She's in Denver now. Speaking of Denver, the flights are absurd.
Speaking of being late, we should probably leave.
Speaking of money, the deposit hasn't cleared.
entries.русский: кстати о, раз уж речь зашла о — разг. связка при смене темы
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or the fused relative which (speaking of which); never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: Speaking of [noun phrase], [clause] · Speaking of which, [clause] — essentially always sentence-initial
entries.variants: talking of (chiefly British); speaking of which (fixed); which reminds me (the non-prepositional equivalent)
entries.contrast: It is a topic-shift device, not a framing preposition: it claims that the object was just mentioned and uses that mention as a bridge to something new. As for also shifts topic, but it returns to one item out of a set already under discussion rather than following an association. By origin this is a dangling participle — nobody is doing the speaking — but it has grammaticalized completely, and no usage authority requires a matching subject.
entries.see also: as for, apropos of, on the subject of, regarding

entries.meaning: Names the human being a document is meant to reach, as distinct from the address it is mailed to and the subject it is about. It is one of the three labels stacked at the top of a business letter, and the only one that points at a person.
examples: Please send the signed original to the attention of the claims department.
Address the appeal to the attention of the hearing officer, not to the clerk.
The check was mailed to the attention of Ms. Okafor in payroll.
The envelope was marked Attn: Facilities, Third Floor.
Fax it to the number on the letterhead, Attn: Kimberly Voss.
The error came to the attention of the auditors only in March.
Nothing of the kind was ever brought to the attention of the board.

senses.head: Routing a document to the person meant to act on it
body: The core sense, and the one that governs a real object.
examples: Please send the signed original to the attention of the claims department.
Address the appeal to the attention of the hearing officer, not to the clerk.
The check was mailed to the attention of Ms. Okafor in payroll.

senses.head: As the written label on an envelope, a fax cover sheet, or a shipping form
body: Written Attn: or ATTN:, capitalized and closed with a colon.
examples: The envelope was marked Attn: Facilities, Third Floor.
Fax it to the number on the letterhead, Attn: Kimberly Voss.

senses.head: Come to the attention of — the passive frame, where nothing is being routed
body: It means only that somebody noticed.
examples: The error came to the attention of the auditors only in March.
Nothing of the kind was ever brought to the attention of the board.

entries.pronunciation note: too-thee-uh-TEN-shun-uv · the abbreviation Attn: is read aloud as attention, never letter by letter
entries.русский: вниманию (кого-л.) — адресация документа исполнителю; на конверте пишут Attn:
entries.register: formal, business and administrative correspondence; the Attn: form is a written label only and never appears in speech
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a person, office, or department — a name, a title, a desk. No gerund and no clause of any kind (✗ to the attention of that the invoice is late). Pronoun objects give way to the possessive frame: bring it to my attention, it came to her attention, and ✗ to the attention of me is not English.
entries.pattern: [send / direct / address / forward / bring] [object] to the attention of [person] · heading: Attn: [name] · possessive: to [possessive] attention
entries.variants: Attn: and ATTN: — the envelope, fax-cover, and mailroom abbreviation, conventionally closed with a colon; for the attention of and FAO, which are British; attention: spelled out, common on shipping labels; and the possessive to my attention, to his attention, which is the ordinary conversational form
entries.contrast: Two labels sit in the same block of a business letter and do opposite jobs: re names the subject and this one names the reader. Distinguish it also from care of and its abbreviation c/o, which name an intermediary who holds the mail for somebody else rather than the person meant to act on it — c/o is an address, Attn: is an instruction — and which are treated with the complex and multi-word prepositions. Note finally the quite different passive frame come to the attention of, where nobody is routing anything and the phrase just means "was noticed by."
entries.see also: re, in re, in reference to, in the matter of, on behalf of
